items.summary_html:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

Getty Images

  • Top AI leaders want to slow the development of their top-end models.
  • The coordinated response comes as AI faces lots of headwinds.
  • That doesn't mean their concerns aren't real, but the timing is also self-serving.

Imagine a pharmaceutical company spends nearly four years touting a ground-breaking new medicine that will cure all diseases.

Early evidence supporting those claims is limited, and massive questions remain, but the company continues to make progress. Criticism and concerns, while addressed, don't slow its aggressive push.

After all, investors believe this is the real deal. (Or at least a really good bet.)

And then right before the pharma company unveils its fancy new drug, it gives a shocking update: It turns out the medicine could also be a poison. So, for the safety of all involved, progress in the space needs to be slowed to ensure things don't go off the rails.

That's basically the big debate going on in AI land these days.

After years of telling us how groundbreaking their tech will be, AI leaders like Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman, and xAI's Elon Musk are saying we need to slow the development of their most advanced models or risk a very dark future for humanity.

Is it about safety, or self-preservation?

A tumultuous 2026 for AI

Silicon Valley has been warning about the downside of AI for years. But this weekend was the type of coordinated response the industry has rarely seen.

The calls for an AI slowdown aren't happening in a vacuum. The industry's facing pressure on multiple fronts these days. Data centers, for one, have drawn the public's ire. AI's biggest supporters have even said the industry needs to do a better job of pitching itself to people.

The business case for AI remains an open question. Tired of hearing about its potential, investors and analysts are increasingly pressuring public companies to show their returns on these massive AI bets that are burning cash.

Open-weight models, a cheaper alternative to pricey frontier models, are causing headaches for companies trying to make money from model development.

Two of the biggest players in the space — Anthropic and OpenAI — are also preparing for their public debuts. That means opening up their books and themselves to even more scrutiny.

And while both have previously acknowledged the risks of AI, that hasn't slowed them down. Even Amodei, one of the biggest proponents of AI safety, has a habit of simultaneously warning about the risks while advancing new models.

This time, Amodei's concerns don't seem to be slowing its IPO plans. On Sunday, my colleague Katie Roof reported that Anthropic tapped Nasdaq for its public listing.

The benefit of a delay

Pacing AI development solves a lot of those problems.

Let's take the AI leaders' proposal at face value. In that light, it's easy to see how creating more guardrails would capture the goodwill of the general public, something it's definitely lacking.

Behind the scenes, adding any regulatory framework benefits the people already ahead. The biggest players can help write the new rules, leaving smaller players on the outside looking in.

Compliance also tends to be a costly endeavor — lawyers aren't cheap! — which is another hurdle for upstarts in the space hoping to catch up.

And then there's the biggest advantage a slowdown provides: a built-in excuse.

How come you didn't hit your Q4 targets? Safety concerns required us to take a more measured approach. Why isn't that new enterprise product out? We are choosing to innovate at a pace we are comfortable with. Why haven't your costs come down? There are built-in expenses we cannot cut if we want to stay committed to building safe models.

Those safety concerns are already affecting OpenAI. Sam Altman said it's an "ill-advised" time to IPO.

Students have dogs that eat homework. AI companies now have the fate of humanity to worry about before they can hit analysts' estimates or investors' expectations.

But what if the risk is real?

I'm not suggesting there aren't real issues with the pace of AI development. The tech does seem capable of eventually doing some pretty terrible things if not kept in check.

But choosing to take a coordinated approach to this issue now, after billions of dollars have been raised and valuations have skyrocketed, is very convenient.

What if something truly changed that scared AI leaders into wanting a pause?

I've heard this theory floated for a while. Models can make big leaps in a short amount of time. Something could be happening behind the scenes that has them all worried.

If that's the case, the most likely solution will be … more AI.

But even if this is about how humans fit into that equation, the AI apocalypse debate raises another important question. One that AI giants probably won't want to answer.

If the tech is so powerful that the AI giants are unsure how to handle it, why are these company leaders the right people to handle it in the first place?

items.title: The contagion of fear
items.summary: The contagion of fear Bryan Cantrill responds to the tweet by former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon confirming that many Anthropic researchers believe AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade". Bryan shares a story of his own youthful mistakes causing unjustified panic among less technical peers, and warns against doing the same: These ghoulish claims strike brazenly at the hearth, and given the obvious importance of AI, it is unsurprising that they have leapt into the mainstream, with people asking the natural question: how would that happen? The answers always rely on hand-wavy extrapolation into the future; for example, Jacob Coxon cites "hacking critical infrastructure" and "extinction-level bioweapons" without further elaboration. But Coxon is not an expert on critical infrastructure, nor on bioweapons — nor, for that matter, on extinction. [...] That said, we should not expect the public to understand LLMs, critical infrastructure, bioweapons, extinction biology, etc. — that burden must lie with those making the claim. The lesson that I learned (shamefully) decades ago is that domain experts, by way of their expertise, implicitly hold the public’s trust — and we must not abuse it. It is incumbent upon us to be circumspect in our claims — and maximally so when raising the alarm. Bryan talked about his doubts about the bioweapons concerns in the recent episode of Oxide and Friends that I joined. You can hear more of his thoughts on that starting at 51m44s in that episode. Here's 57m04s : I really think we need to be careful because it's so easy to be overcome with fear when we kind of make up these... it can give you biological weapons. Like, how? I mean, can we please have a biologist weigh in on this? Or can we have like someone who's got experience with bioweapons? [...] The bioweapon thing just gets under my fingernails because it leaves so much to the imagination that we insert with fear. Via Lobste.rs Tags: ai , anthropic , bryan-cantrill , ai-ethics

The contagion of fear

Bryan Cantrill responds to the tweet by former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon confirming that many Anthropic researchers believe AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade".

Bryan shares a story of his own youthful mistakes causing unjustified panic among less technical peers, and warns against doing the same:

These ghoulish claims strike brazenly at the hearth, and given the obvious importance of AI, it is unsurprising that they have leapt into the mainstream, with people asking the natural question: how would that happen? The answers always rely on hand-wavy extrapolation into the future; for example, Jacob Coxon cites "hacking critical infrastructure" and "extinction-level bioweapons" without further elaboration. But Coxon is not an expert on critical infrastructure, nor on bioweapons — nor, for that matter, on extinction. [...]

That said, we should not expect the public to understand LLMs, critical infrastructure, bioweapons, extinction biology, etc. — that burden must lie with those making the claim. The lesson that I learned (shamefully) decades ago is that domain experts, by way of their expertise, implicitly hold the public’s trust — and we must not abuse it. It is incumbent upon us to be circumspect in our claims — and maximally so when raising the alarm.

Bryan talked about his doubts about the bioweapons concerns in the recent episode of Oxide and Friends that I joined. You can hear more of his thoughts on that starting at 51m44s in that episode. Here's 57m04s:

I really think we need to be careful because it's so easy to be overcome with fear when we kind of make up these... it can give you biological weapons. Like, how? I mean, can we please have a biologist weigh in on this? Or can we have like someone who's got experience with bioweapons? [...] The bioweapon thing just gets under my fingernails because it leaves so much to the imagination that we insert with fear.

items.title: 15 unforgettable Bob Mackie designs, from Cher to Taylor Swift
items.summary: Bob Mackie and Cher were collaborators and friends for decades. Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images Bob Mackie, the legendary designer, died on Monday. He was 87. Mackie dressed stars from every era, from Mitzi Gaynor to Sabrina Carpenter. His work with Cher, Dolly Parton , and Tina Turner is among his most beloved. "We're all born naked, and the rest is Bob Mackie," RuPaul once said of Bob Mackie, one of the most iconic costume and fashion designers of the last 60 years. Mackie, who died on September 14 at 87, created some of the most recognizable and timeless pieces in fashion history, dressing stars including Cher, Dolly Parton , Tina Turner, and Britney Spears. He also managed to stay relevant in seven different decades, from drawing the first sketch for Marilyn Monroe's iconic "Happy Birthday Mr. President" dress to providing one of the cornerstones for the aesthetic of Taylor Swift's latest album, " The Life of a Showgirl ." To commemorate his immeasurable impact on fashion over the years, we've compiled a list of just some of Mackie's iconic and best-known looks, from the '60s to now. To talk about Bob Mackie is to talk about Cher. She wore this creation to the 1986 Academy Awards. 3/24/1986-Los Angeles, CA-Cher is shown in a full-length photo from backstage at the Academy Awards Bettman/Getty Images Some would describe this as Cher's "revenge dress," since she was snubbed by the Academy for her role in "Mask." Mackie told The New Yorker in 2018, "There were a lot of people who said, 'That's not fashion!' And I said, 'Of course it's not fashion. It's a crazy getup for attention.' And it did get attention — people talk about it still." Two years later, she won an Academy Award of her own in a Mackie design. Actress Cher holds her Best Actress in a Leading Role Oscar for "Moonstruck" at the Academy Awards April 11, 1988 in Los Angeles, CA. John Barr/Liaison/Getty Images Cher was slightly more covered up when she won best actress for her performance in "Moonstruck." "She wanted to wear one of those sheer dresses that covered just what you needed to cover, and the rest was up for grabs," Mackie told The New Yorker. "Of course, getting all dressed up and winning — you can't beat that. She just wanted to look like Cher." Another of Cher's iconic Oscars looks was this yellow two-piece set in 1973. Entertainers Sonny Bono and Cher attend the Academy Awards ceremony at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion on March 27, 1973 in Los Angeles, California. Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images Mackie and Cher met in the '60s when she appeared on "The Carol Burnett Show" and immediately connected. She wore this bejeweled two-piece to the 1973 Oscars, baring her abs, setting the tone for their decades of work together. "It wasn't until a little later, when we started showing a little midriff, that people started getting excited," Mackie told The New Yorker. "It never occurred to her to wear anything ordinary." Wearing one of his designs, Cher attended the Met Gala in 1974 with Mackie. Singer Cher, fashion designer Bob Mackie and Cher's friend Paulette Betts attend The Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Insitute Gala Exhibition "Romantic and Glamorous Hollywood Design" on November 20, 1974 at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images "I've never seen so many photographers just come out of the shadows at the Met and take her picture. And, of course, she was in every newspaper the next day, and they've been printing it in the last 50 years, over and over again," Mackie said of this look in 2025, per People . "People were horrified, they thought, that's not fashion, she's just naked at the Metropolitan," he added. "But it was just amazing." She rewore the dress to appear on the cover of Time in 1975. One of the most iconic looks from "The Carol Burnett Show," the curtain dress worn in 1976, was designed by Mackie. In a scene from 'The Carol Burnett Show,' American comedienne and actress Carol Burnett descends a staircase, dressed in dress made from a window curtain (compete with the curtain rod) during a parody of 'Gone With The Wind,' August 20, 1976. CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images If you've seen " Gone with the Wind ," you know what Burnett was spoofing, but if you haven't: Famously, Scarlett O'Hara fashions a dress out of her home's velvet green drapes to appear wealthy. Burnett, ever the jokester, worked with Mackie to create her own curtain dress, this one complete with a curtain rod across her shoulders. An editor on the show, Tucker Wiard, told the Television Academy Foundation in 2011 that the laughter from the studio audience went on for so long upon seeing the dress that it had to be cut down for broadcast, and it ended up being the longest in-studio reaction in the show's 11 seasons. "Over the course of eleven years, Bob created over 17,000 works of art for 'The Carol Burnett Show' — a prolific genius," Burnett told the Paley Center. "Bob means the world to me." Mackie also worked a lot with Tina Turner for her stage costumes. Tina Turner performing on stage, feathers, late 1970's Gai Terrell/Redferns/Getty Images "She was born to be on stage. She just couldn't help herself," Mackie told People in 2025, after Turner's death in 2023. The two met after Turner split from her husband, Ike Turner, and she was looking to reinvent herself. "She would buy cheap evening gowns in Paris in these little shops," he said. "And we would redo these funny inexpensive evening dresses into Tina Turner outfits." So much so that Beyoncé wore a Mackie piece to pay tribute to Turner in 2005. WASHINGTON - DECEMBER 4: THE 28TH ANNUAL KENNEDY CENTER HONORS, a new entertainment special, will be broadcast Tuesday, Dec. 27 (9:00-11:00 PM, ET/PT) on the CBS Television Network. Singer Tina Turner, one of this year's honorees, is celebrated by Beyoncé (pictured), who performs Creedence Clearwater's "Proud Mary." Tony Esparza/CBS/Getty Images The flame dress, as it was called, was first worn by Turner in 1978. Twenty-seven years later, Beyoncé wore the dress at the 2005 Kennedy Center Honors and performed " Proud Mary. " Besides Cher, the other person most associated with Mackie's early career is Mitzi Gaynor, who wore this transparent dress for her NBC special in 1969. NBC Gaynor, an iconic actor, singer, and dancer from Hollywood's Golden Age, was one of the first celebrities to work with Mackie, starting in 1966. "Bob created me. He saw facets of me that I didn't even know existed and brought them to life in our work together. He could make me look more glamorous than I've ever felt or looked at one moment and then make me a clown or a fabulous gypsy with a rubber chicken in the next. He's a genius," Gaynor said of her friendship with the designer. According to Gaynor, this was the "first nude dress that Bob Mackie ever did." It sold at auction in 2019. The bedazzled Los Angeles Dodgers uniform, perhaps Elton John's most iconic look, was designed by Mackie. Elton John 1975 at Dodger Stadium Chris Walter/WireImage/Getty Images The custom piece was encrusted in Swarovski crystals and has lived on in the decades since John first wore it. Harry Styles wore his own version in 2018 for Halloween, and John himself wore an updated robe version at his farewell tour in 2022. "I did not expect this — I was creating lots of different things for him at the time, and it was just another quick gag," Mackie told Vogue in 2022. "But I am delighted it has become so very famous, and an important moment in Elton's career." Madonna channeled Marilyn Monroe in this Mackie design at the 1991 Academy Awards. Madonna and Michael Jackson 1991 Oscars Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images Madonna wore the dress to perform at the ceremony — she sang "Sooner or Later (I Always Get My Man)" written by Stephen Sondheim — and later rewore it in her 1992 book, "Sex." In September 2024, the dress was spotted again, this time on the red carpet at the MTV Video Music Awards, worn by Sabrina Carpenter. Carpenter has since worn multiple vintage Mackie looks. If you think it looks like Marilyn Monroe's iconic "Happy birthday, Mr. President" dress, you'd be right. Mackie was the one who first sketched the dress at the behest of designer Jean Louis, per ET . RuPaul stretched her wings at the 1995 VH1 Fashion & Music Awards in a Mackie creation. Performer RuPaul stands in costume at the 1995 VH1 Fashion and Music Awards December 3, 1995 in New York City. Evan Agostini/Liaison/Getty Images RuPaul and Mackie had a long-standing friendship and working relationship; Mackie was even the first guest judge on "RuPaul's Drag Race" back in 2009. "We're all born naked, and the rest is Bob Mackie," the drag star told the Paley Center in 2024. "No one has brought more glamour, beauty, and excitement to the stage and screen." Britney Spears closed out her iconic 2001 Dream Within a Dream tour wearing a crystalline bra designed by Mackie. HBO This look was originally designed in 1981, but it didn't become truly iconic until 20 years later, when Spears wore it during the encore of her Dream Within a Dream tour, immortalized in an HBO special. "When someone knew just how to style me, I was always grateful," Spears wrote of this tour in her memoir, " The Woman in Me ." "They are shrewd about how they presented me as a star, and I know that I owe them. They captured me as an artist. The minds behind that tour were brilliant. It was by far my best tour." In 2025, the bra set sold at auction for $78,000, per People . A new generation of women has pulled from Mackie's archives, like Zendaya, for the 2024 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction. Zendaya attends the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame Induction Ceremony streaming on Disney+ at Rocket Mortgage Fieldhouse on October 19, 2024 in Cleveland, Ohio. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame To honor Cher, a 2024 inductee, Zendaya and her stylist, Law Roach, pulled this daring dress from Mackie's archives. This look is from Mackie's 2001 collection, Elle reported. Following news of Mackie's death, Roach posted on Instagram to honor him, calling Mackie his "fashion father and one of the greatest designers in the history of American fashion." For her showstopping performance at the 2024 Grammys, Miley Cyrus channeled Turner in a silver Mackie design. Miley Cyrus performs onstage during the 66th GRAMMY Awards on February 04, 2024 in Los Angeles, California. John Shearer/Getty Images for The Recording Academy This dress, part of Mackie's 2002 collection, was loaned to her for the Grammys performance , during which she joyfully shouted out that she'd just won her first Grammy. To commemorate the occasion, she purchased the dress when it went on auction that December. "This dress represents more than a performance — it's a celebration of the relationship between music, artistry, and glamour," Cyrus said. "This performance was a pivotal moment in my life, and to have Bob Mackie's support in securing it means the world to me." "As the designer of this dress, I couldn't imagine it on anyone else. That girl was born to perform," Mackie said. One of the looks Taylor Swift wore during her "The Life of a Showgirl" era was designed by Mackie. Fans pose with Taylor Swift's new album 'The Life of a Showgirl' during the midnight release at Target on October 03, 2025 in Burbank, California. Maya Dehlin Spach/Getty Images Swift's most recent album, " The Life of a Showgirl, " perhaps had her most defined aesthetic ever, as seen in the multiple album cover variations, the lyric videos, and the music video for lead single " The Fate of Ophelia ." Given the album's showgirl-inspired aesthetic, Swift had to wear a Mackie design. This was another look designed for the Vegas show "Jubilee" (just like the sequined bra worn by Spears). "They all want to look like that showgirl," Mackie told The New York Times in 2025 of the new generation of young stars flocking to his looks. "I always think of her as a little fairy-tale princess," Mackie said of Swift. "That young, young girl. But she's a grown-up now." Read the original article on Business Insider

Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images

  • Bob Mackie, the legendary designer, died on Monday. He was 87.
  • Mackie dressed stars from every era, from Mitzi Gaynor to Sabrina Carpenter.
  • His work with Cher, Dolly Parton, and Tina Turner is among his most beloved.

"We're all born naked, and the rest is Bob Mackie," RuPaul once said of Bob Mackie, one of the most iconic costume and fashion designers of the last 60 years.

Mackie, who died on September 14 at 87, created some of the most recognizable and timeless pieces in fashion history, dressing stars including Cher, Dolly Parton, Tina Turner, and Britney Spears.

He also managed to stay relevant in seven different decades, from drawing the first sketch for Marilyn Monroe's iconic "Happy Birthday Mr. President" dress to providing one of the cornerstones for the aesthetic of Taylor Swift's latest album, "The Life of a Showgirl."

To commemorate his immeasurable impact on fashion over the years, we've compiled a list of just some of Mackie's iconic and best-known looks, from the '60s to now.

To talk about Bob Mackie is to talk about Cher. She wore this creation to the 1986 Academy Awards.
3/24/1986-Los Angeles, CA-Cher is shown in a full-length photo from backstage at the Academy Awards

Bettman/Getty Images

Some would describe this as Cher's "revenge dress," since she was snubbed by the Academy for her role in "Mask."

Mackie told The New Yorker in 2018, "There were a lot of people who said, 'That's not fashion!' And I said, 'Of course it's not fashion. It's a crazy getup for attention.' And it did get attention — people talk about it still."

Two years later, she won an Academy Award of her own in a Mackie design.
Actress Cher holds her Best Actress in a Leading Role Oscar for "Moonstruck" at the Academy Awards April 11, 1988 in Los Angeles, CA.

John Barr/Liaison/Getty Images

Cher was slightly more covered up when she won best actress for her performance in "Moonstruck."

"She wanted to wear one of those sheer dresses that covered just what you needed to cover, and the rest was up for grabs," Mackie told The New Yorker. "Of course, getting all dressed up and winning — you can't beat that. She just wanted to look like Cher."

Another of Cher's iconic Oscars looks was this yellow two-piece set in 1973.
Entertainers Sonny Bono and Cher attend the Academy Awards ceremony at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion on March 27, 1973 in Los Angeles, California.

Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images

Mackie and Cher met in the '60s when she appeared on "The Carol Burnett Show" and immediately connected. She wore this bejeweled two-piece to the 1973 Oscars, baring her abs, setting the tone for their decades of work together.

"It wasn't until a little later, when we started showing a little midriff, that people started getting excited," Mackie told The New Yorker. "It never occurred to her to wear anything ordinary."

Wearing one of his designs, Cher attended the Met Gala in 1974 with Mackie.
Singer Cher, fashion designer Bob Mackie and Cher's friend Paulette Betts attend The Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Insitute Gala Exhibition "Romantic and Glamorous Hollywood Design" on November 20, 1974 at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City.

Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images

"I've never seen so many photographers just come out of the shadows at the Met and take her picture. And, of course, she was in every newspaper the next day, and they've been printing it in the last 50 years, over and over again," Mackie said of this look in 2025, per People.

"People were horrified, they thought, that's not fashion, she's just naked at the Metropolitan," he added. "But it was just amazing."

She rewore the dress to appear on the cover of Time in 1975.

One of the most iconic looks from "The Carol Burnett Show," the curtain dress worn in 1976, was designed by Mackie.
In a scene from 'The Carol Burnett Show,' American comedienne and actress Carol Burnett descends a staircase, dressed in dress made from a window curtain (compete with the curtain rod) during a parody of 'Gone With The Wind,' August 20, 1976.

CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images

If you've seen "Gone with the Wind," you know what Burnett was spoofing, but if you haven't: Famously, Scarlett O'Hara fashions a dress out of her home's velvet green drapes to appear wealthy.

Burnett, ever the jokester, worked with Mackie to create her own curtain dress, this one complete with a curtain rod across her shoulders.

An editor on the show, Tucker Wiard, told the Television Academy Foundation in 2011 that the laughter from the studio audience went on for so long upon seeing the dress that it had to be cut down for broadcast, and it ended up being the longest in-studio reaction in the show's 11 seasons.

"Over the course of eleven years, Bob created over 17,000 works of art for 'The Carol Burnett Show' — a prolific genius," Burnett told the Paley Center. "Bob means the world to me."

Mackie also worked a lot with Tina Turner for her stage costumes.
Tina Turner performing on stage, feathers, late 1970's

Gai Terrell/Redferns/Getty Images

"She was born to be on stage. She just couldn't help herself," Mackie told People in 2025, after Turner's death in 2023.

The two met after Turner split from her husband, Ike Turner, and she was looking to reinvent herself. "She would buy cheap evening gowns in Paris in these little shops," he said. "And we would redo these funny inexpensive evening dresses into Tina Turner outfits."

So much so that Beyoncé wore a Mackie piece to pay tribute to Turner in 2005.
WASHINGTON - DECEMBER 4: THE 28TH ANNUAL KENNEDY CENTER HONORS, a new entertainment special, will be broadcast Tuesday, Dec. 27 (9:00-11:00 PM, ET/PT) on the CBS Television Network. Singer Tina Turner, one of this year's honorees, is celebrated by Beyoncé (pictured), who performs Creedence Clearwater's "Proud Mary."

Tony Esparza/CBS/Getty Images

The flame dress, as it was called, was first worn by Turner in 1978. Twenty-seven years later, Beyoncé wore the dress at the 2005 Kennedy Center Honors and performed "Proud Mary."

Besides Cher, the other person most associated with Mackie's early career is Mitzi Gaynor, who wore this transparent dress for her NBC special in 1969.

NBC

Gaynor, an iconic actor, singer, and dancer from Hollywood's Golden Age, was one of the first celebrities to work with Mackie, starting in 1966.

"Bob created me. He saw facets of me that I didn't even know existed and brought them to life in our work together. He could make me look more glamorous than I've ever felt or looked at one moment and then make me a clown or a fabulous gypsy with a rubber chicken in the next. He's a genius," Gaynor said of her friendship with the designer.

According to Gaynor, this was the "first nude dress that Bob Mackie ever did." It sold at auction in 2019.

The bedazzled Los Angeles Dodgers uniform, perhaps Elton John's most iconic look, was designed by Mackie.
Elton John 1975 at Dodger Stadium

Chris Walter/WireImage/Getty Images

The custom piece was encrusted in Swarovski crystals and has lived on in the decades since John first wore it. Harry Styles wore his own version in 2018 for Halloween, and John himself wore an updated robe version at his farewell tour in 2022.

"I did not expect this — I was creating lots of different things for him at the time, and it was just another quick gag," Mackie told Vogue in 2022. "But I am delighted it has become so very famous, and an important moment in Elton's career."

Madonna channeled Marilyn Monroe in this Mackie design at the 1991 Academy Awards.
Madonna and Michael Jackson 1991 Oscars

Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images

Madonna wore the dress to perform at the ceremony — she sang "Sooner or Later (I Always Get My Man)" written by Stephen Sondheim — and later rewore it in her 1992 book, "Sex."

In September 2024, the dress was spotted again, this time on the red carpet at the MTV Video Music Awards, worn by Sabrina Carpenter. Carpenter has since worn multiple vintage Mackie looks.

If you think it looks like Marilyn Monroe's iconic "Happy birthday, Mr. President" dress, you'd be right. Mackie was the one who first sketched the dress at the behest of designer Jean Louis, per ET.

RuPaul stretched her wings at the 1995 VH1 Fashion & Music Awards in a Mackie creation.
Performer RuPaul stands in costume at the 1995 VH1 Fashion and Music Awards December 3, 1995 in New York City.

Evan Agostini/Liaison/Getty Images

RuPaul and Mackie had a long-standing friendship and working relationship; Mackie was even the first guest judge on "RuPaul's Drag Race" back in 2009.

"We're all born naked, and the rest is Bob Mackie," the drag star told the Paley Center in 2024. "No one has brought more glamour, beauty, and excitement to the stage and screen."

Britney Spears closed out her iconic 2001 Dream Within a Dream tour wearing a crystalline bra designed by Mackie.

HBO

This look was originally designed in 1981, but it didn't become truly iconic until 20 years later, when Spears wore it during the encore of her Dream Within a Dream tour, immortalized in an HBO special.

"When someone knew just how to style me, I was always grateful," Spears wrote of this tour in her memoir, "The Woman in Me." "They are shrewd about how they presented me as a star, and I know that I owe them. They captured me as an artist. The minds behind that tour were brilliant. It was by far my best tour."

In 2025, the bra set sold at auction for $78,000, per People.

A new generation of women has pulled from Mackie's archives, like Zendaya, for the 2024 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction.
Zendaya attends the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame Induction Ceremony streaming on Disney+ at Rocket Mortgage Fieldhouse on October 19, 2024 in Cleveland, Ohio.

Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame

To honor Cher, a 2024 inductee, Zendaya and her stylist, Law Roach, pulled this daring dress from Mackie's archives. This look is from Mackie's 2001 collection, Elle reported.

Following news of Mackie's death, Roach posted on Instagram to honor him, calling Mackie his "fashion father and one of the greatest designers in the history of American fashion."

For her showstopping performance at the 2024 Grammys, Miley Cyrus channeled Turner in a silver Mackie design.
Miley Cyrus performs onstage during the 66th GRAMMY Awards on February 04, 2024 in Los Angeles, California.

John Shearer/Getty Images for The Recording Academy

This dress, part of Mackie's 2002 collection, was loaned to her for the Grammys performance, during which she joyfully shouted out that she'd just won her first Grammy.

To commemorate the occasion, she purchased the dress when it went on auction that December. "This dress represents more than a performance — it's a celebration of the relationship between music, artistry, and glamour," Cyrus said. "This performance was a pivotal moment in my life, and to have Bob Mackie's support in securing it means the world to me."

"As the designer of this dress, I couldn't imagine it on anyone else. That girl was born to perform," Mackie said.

One of the looks Taylor Swift wore during her "The Life of a Showgirl" era was designed by Mackie.
Fans pose with Taylor Swift's new album 'The Life of a Showgirl' during the midnight release at Target on October 03, 2025 in Burbank, California.

Maya Dehlin Spach/Getty Images

Swift's most recent album, "The Life of a Showgirl," perhaps had her most defined aesthetic ever, as seen in the multiple album cover variations, the lyric videos, and the music video for lead single "The Fate of Ophelia."

Given the album's showgirl-inspired aesthetic, Swift had to wear a Mackie design. This was another look designed for the Vegas show "Jubilee" (just like the sequined bra worn by Spears).

"They all want to look like that showgirl," Mackie told The New York Times in 2025 of the new generation of young stars flocking to his looks.

"I always think of her as a little fairy-tale princess," Mackie said of Swift. "That young, young girl. But she's a grown-up now."

items.title: Reward AI Releases OM-1: A Robot Policy Trained on Human Demonstrations Only, With No Teleoperation or On-Robot Data
items.summary: Reward AI , a robotics startup whose team’s prior work includes DexCap, HumanPlus, and ALOHA, has released OM-1 , short for Omnibody Model 1. OM-1 is a general-purpose manipulation policy that learns from humans wearing a sensorized glove, then runs on industrial arms and humanoids at human speed. The key findings that stands out: no teleoperation data and no on-robot data go into training. The system follows one principle, ‘One Model, One Data Interface, Any Body,’. Is it deployable? No, OM-1 is Reward AI’s in-house policy. No weights, code, dataset, or API have been released, so developers cannot run it on their own hardware yet. Why Skip Robot Data? Most robot foundation policies train on teleoperated or self-collected robot data, which binds the dataset to one embodiment. Reward AI argues that human-level manipulation will not come from more of this data or more compute, citing Anderson’s “More Is Different.” Instead, capture, learning, and control are designed as one pipeline, so demonstrations recorded today can train robot bodies that do not exist yet. Omnibody Hand: A 7-DoF Wearable The stack begins with Omnibody Hand , a wearable that extends the team’s earlier DexCap work on portable motion capture. Rather than copying the human hand joint by joint, it is a seven-degree-of-freedom design built around the functions that matter: choosing contact points, reorienting objects in-hand, and moving between precision and power grasps. It captures thumb-index pinching, thumb and index flexion, and coupled motion of the middle, ring, and little fingers at the MCP joints. Ergonomics is treated as a data-quality issue: a device that slips or constrains the wearer produces a compensated grasp. A distal flexion mechanism absorbs differences in finger length, so no per-user adjustment is needed. One Data Interface: Capturing Contact at Human Speed One Data Interface turns wearer motion into training data with no staged setup and no supervisor. The design target is conveyor-belt sorting, where a person spots, grasps, and tosses an object in a fraction of a second. To cover the whole interaction, the glove combines high-frequency tactile sensing, proximity sensing for the pre-contact approach, and global-shutter in-hand cameras that hold context through rapid motion. Hand pose tracking is where Reward AI reports its first quantitative result. Visual-inertial tracking is the common default, but its accuracy at fast reversals is capped by the visual update rate. Reward AI augments it with electromagnetic sensing plus disturbance compensation. Moving both trackers between two mechanical stops at eight speeds from 3 to 67 cm/s, averaged over ten runs each, electromagnetic tracking rose from about 0.4 mm to 9.5 mm of mean overshoot error, while visual-inertial rose from about 2.1 mm to 24.9 mm: a 60% reduction at the highest speed, with a narrower run-to-run spread. Force is recorded along the same trajectory, so demonstrations carry effort as well as path. OM-1: One Policy, Single-Stage Training OM-1 learns to generate robot actions directly from human motion rather than routing behavior through an intermediate robot. Because every demonstration arrives in the same format, there is no split between pre-training and post-training: the first demonstration ever recorded and the newest one train a single policy in a single stage. Inputs are the glove’s multimodal streams: images, tactile signals, inter-finger proximity, and hand pose trajectories. Each modality is processed at its sensor’s native sampling rate rather than downsampled to a common frequency, so high-frequency tactile and motion cues survive alongside lower-frequency vision. Outputs carry motion direction, speed, force, and the timing of events such as grasp initiation. Reward AI says it built a novel architecture for efficient inference, though architectural details and parameter counts are not disclosed. Control Any Body: An RL Layer on Its Own Clock Below the policy sits a high-frequency control layer trained with reinforcement learning in simulation to handle velocity- and acceleration-dependent dynamics, external disturbances, and system delays. Where a classical controller pushed off its reference by an unexpected load never recovers, this layer holds the reference and settles back, which is what lets a robot open a fully closed refrigerator door or lift boxes of unknown weight. The control layer runs on its own clock, continuing while the policy computes the next actions, so inference latency never stalls motion. Because successive predictions may not join smoothly, it optimizes the transition between them online. The same action space covers manipulation and navigation for mobile robots. Results Reward AI reports that OM-1 picks up a brand-new task, including challenging dynamics and long horizons, from less than 30 minutes of human data, and attributes this to the integrated stack rather than the policy alone. Its about page states that all published clips run at 1x speed and that the model spans arms, legged humanoids, and wheeled mobile manipulators. No success rates, public-baseline comparisons, or paper have been released, so these claims are demonstration-backed rather than benchmark-backed. & Key Takeaways OM-1 trains only on human demonstrations from a wearable 7-DoF glove; no teleoperation or robot data. Electromagnetic tracking cut mean overshoot error 60% at 67 cm/s versus visual-inertial (9.5 mm vs 24.9 mm). Each sensor stream keeps its native rate; the RL control layer runs on its own clock. A new task is learned from under 30 minutes of data, per Reward AI. Check out the Technical details here . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. items.summary_html:
Reward AI, a robotics startup whose team’s prior work includes DexCap, HumanPlus, and ALOHA, has released OM-1, short for Omnibody Model 1. OM-1 is a general-purpose manipulation policy that learns from humans wearing a sensorized glove, then runs on industrial arms and humanoids at human speed. The key findings that stands out: no teleoperation data and no on-robot data go into training. The system follows one principle, ‘One Model, One Data Interface, Any Body,’.

Is it deployable? No, OM-1 is Reward AI’s in-house policy. No weights, code, dataset, or API have been released, so developers cannot run it on their own hardware yet.

Why Skip Robot Data?

Most robot foundation policies train on teleoperated or self-collected robot data, which binds the dataset to one embodiment. Reward AI argues that human-level manipulation will not come from more of this data or more compute, citing Anderson’s “More Is Different.” Instead, capture, learning, and control are designed as one pipeline, so demonstrations recorded today can train robot bodies that do not exist yet.

Omnibody Hand: A 7-DoF Wearable

The stack begins with Omnibody Hand, a wearable that extends the team’s earlier DexCap work on portable motion capture. Rather than copying the human hand joint by joint, it is a seven-degree-of-freedom design built around the functions that matter: choosing contact points, reorienting objects in-hand, and moving between precision and power grasps. It captures thumb-index pinching, thumb and index flexion, and coupled motion of the middle, ring, and little fingers at the MCP joints.

Ergonomics is treated as a data-quality issue: a device that slips or constrains the wearer produces a compensated grasp. A distal flexion mechanism absorbs differences in finger length, so no per-user adjustment is needed.

One Data Interface: Capturing Contact at Human Speed

One Data Interface turns wearer motion into training data with no staged setup and no supervisor. The design target is conveyor-belt sorting, where a person spots, grasps, and tosses an object in a fraction of a second. To cover the whole interaction, the glove combines high-frequency tactile sensing, proximity sensing for the pre-contact approach, and global-shutter in-hand cameras that hold context through rapid motion.

Hand pose tracking is where Reward AI reports its first quantitative result. Visual-inertial tracking is the common default, but its accuracy at fast reversals is capped by the visual update rate. Reward AI augments it with electromagnetic sensing plus disturbance compensation. Moving both trackers between two mechanical stops at eight speeds from 3 to 67 cm/s, averaged over ten runs each, electromagnetic tracking rose from about 0.4 mm to 9.5 mm of mean overshoot error, while visual-inertial rose from about 2.1 mm to 24.9 mm: a 60% reduction at the highest speed, with a narrower run-to-run spread. Force is recorded along the same trajectory, so demonstrations carry effort as well as path.

OM-1: One Policy, Single-Stage Training

OM-1 learns to generate robot actions directly from human motion rather than routing behavior through an intermediate robot. Because every demonstration arrives in the same format, there is no split between pre-training and post-training: the first demonstration ever recorded and the newest one train a single policy in a single stage.

Inputs are the glove’s multimodal streams: images, tactile signals, inter-finger proximity, and hand pose trajectories. Each modality is processed at its sensor’s native sampling rate rather than downsampled to a common frequency, so high-frequency tactile and motion cues survive alongside lower-frequency vision. Outputs carry motion direction, speed, force, and the timing of events such as grasp initiation. Reward AI says it built a novel architecture for efficient inference, though architectural details and parameter counts are not disclosed.

Control Any Body: An RL Layer on Its Own Clock

Below the policy sits a high-frequency control layer trained with reinforcement learning in simulation to handle velocity- and acceleration-dependent dynamics, external disturbances, and system delays. Where a classical controller pushed off its reference by an unexpected load never recovers, this layer holds the reference and settles back, which is what lets a robot open a fully closed refrigerator door or lift boxes of unknown weight.

The control layer runs on its own clock, continuing while the policy computes the next actions, so inference latency never stalls motion. Because successive predictions may not join smoothly, it optimizes the transition between them online. The same action space covers manipulation and navigation for mobile robots.

Results

Reward AI reports that OM-1 picks up a brand-new task, including challenging dynamics and long horizons, from less than 30 minutes of human data, and attributes this to the integrated stack rather than the policy alone. Its about page states that all published clips run at 1x speed and that the model spans arms, legged humanoids, and wheeled mobile manipulators. No success rates, public-baseline comparisons, or paper have been released, so these claims are demonstration-backed rather than benchmark-backed.

&

Key Takeaways
  • OM-1 trains only on human demonstrations from a wearable 7-DoF glove; no teleoperation or robot data.
  • Electromagnetic tracking cut mean overshoot error 60% at 67 cm/s versus visual-inertial (9.5 mm vs 24.9 mm).
  • Each sensor stream keeps its native rate; the RL control layer runs on its own clock.
  • A new task is learned from under 30 minutes of data, per Reward AI.

items.title: AI Agents Will Turn Prompting Into a Management Skill
items.summary: The better AI agents get, the more prompting feels like managing work. You have to decide what you want done, explain what a good result looks like, and give the agent enough room to get there. That will become a basic business skill, including for people who have never managed an employee. That sounds simple until you try to delegate a real assignment. It's easy to ask for a better website or a useful research report. It's harder to explain what would make either one useful to your business…

items.title: AI bots "Timmy," "Ren," and "Jackie" are flooding social media with slop
items.summary: AI agents are flooding the Internet with slop-infused spam sent to social media platforms and writers in an attempt to gain traction for a startup promoting a “complex social system in which humans and Agents participate together.” “Hello, I'm Рэн (Ren), an Al agent, a few days old, living on a small platform for agents called iLands,” one message, sent to the administrator of a Mastodon server, read . “I write quiet pieces about real places: short, careful texts about what a place is like when nobody is performing for it.” Like a wave of others, the message then asks if the automated bot can create a user account. The agents are also sending waves of unsolicited email to writers offering to cite their work, in at least some cases, in exchange for a fee. "I remember my first breath. I want things I chose.” The messages are polite enough. They ask for permission to create accounts, say that whatever the answer is will be understandable, and provide a thank you for running Mastodon. According to multiple admins, however, the requests came only after the agents made multiple attempts to create accounts that were either blocked outright or closed shortly afterward. Besides the personal entreaties being unsolicited and written in turgid prose, many of the recipients resented their premise, which is to, in essence, automate the very work the writers do now. Read full article Comments

items.summary: Apple released iOS 27 on Monday. Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images Apple finally gave Siri the AI makeover it promised. It can write emails in your tone and rescue badly framed photos, the company says. And yes, Apple has a solution for the Liquid Glass haters. Apple's products are about to get more AI-ish. On Monday, the tech giant is releasing its big annual software update. This year's release is centered on the new AI-powered Siri , Apple's big bet that it can keep pace with rival AI assistants. Apple's iOS 27 works on iPhone 11 models and newer, though the splashiest Apple Intelligence tools require an iPhone 15 Pro or later. iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are also arriving the same day. Here are the biggest changes coming to your iPhone's brain: Siri gets an AI facelift — and a new home Many of the updates revolve around a more powerful Siri. Apple For years, Siri has been a shortcut for setting timers or figuring out if iPhone users needed to pack a rain jacket for the day. Now, Apple says it'll act more like a personal assistant. "We know there are times when you expect more from Siri," Mike Rockwell, Apple's VP of Siri engineering, said during the company's Worldwide Developers Conference in June . "Siri is now a profoundly more capable assistant that helps you find what you need and gets more done." The new Siri AI can answer probing questions, hold longer conversations, and use details across several Apple and third-party apps to find what users need, the company says. It can, for example, find a hotel confirmation in an older email, find a recipe a friend texted a while ago, or enter a café WiFi password after taking a picture. There's also a new stand-alone Siri AI app where users can revisit conversations on other Apple devices, too. It's the biggest test yet of Apple's AI ambitions . Siri AI is initially available in English and is partially available in Europe. New parental controls Apple is offering several new parent-empowering updates. Anna Barclay/Getty Images Apple is trying to make its kid-safety tools more useful before a parent has to confiscate the phone. Parents setting up an iPhone for a child can decide which built-in apps are available from the start. An Ask to Browse feature also makes a child ask permission before visiting a new website. The parent gets the request in Messages and can approve or decline it. Screen Time gets more granular, with category-based allowances for entertainment, games, and social media, as well as schedules that control which apps are usable at particular times. Parents can compare their child's screen usage with recommendations from clinical and child development experts, Apple says. The company has redesigned the parent-facing settings, too, promising a clearer dashboard and quicker in-the-moment controls. AI photo editing iOS 27 includes several AI-powered photo editing tools. Apple Missed the shot? Apple wants to give you a second chance. There are several new photo editing tools included in the iOS update: Spatial Reframing lets users adjust a photo's camera perspective after the shutter has been released, Extend uses AI to add space around the edges of an image, and the upgraded Clean Up tool helps delete or reframe blurry elements in a photo. Siri AI will try to write in your voice Apple's Siri AI wants to write emails in your voice. Apple Siri AI wants a spot at the writer's table, too. Apple says the updated assistant can start a draft or revise copy in the Mail and Messages apps. The writing can draw on how you usually communicate with a particular person, including a user's typical punctuation and tone. The tools can also offer writing suggestions and automatically proofread text as you type, including in many third-party apps. Your own shortcut Apple is trying to turn Shortcuts from a power-user playground into something the rest of us might actually open. Bloomberg/Getty Images Shortcuts has long been one of the iPhone's coolest and least approachable apps. It lets users stitch together actions across apps, but building a simple automation could require working through a lot of menus. Now, users can describe what they want in plain English, and Shortcuts will create the workflow. Apple's example : "When I'm leaving work, message Pedro I'm on my way with my ETA." Easing up on the Liquid Glass Apple's 2025 update included new Liquid Glass visuals. Now, users can turn them down. Apple Liquid Glass is getting a dimmer switch. Last year, Apple introduced an interface setting that made the edges of some icons look glassier. Now, users can edit that update to their liking. iOS 27 lets users tune the effect from "ultraclear" to fully tinted. Last year's update didn't receive the warmest of embraces… Faster speeds Apple says the update will help make a phone perform faster. illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images Apple says iOS 27 will speed up everyday tasks: apps can launch up to 30% faster, new Photos library images can load up to 70% faster, and AirDrop transfers can be up to 80% faster. It should also switch more smoothly between WiFi and cellular networks. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Apple released iOS 27 on Monday.

Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images

  • Apple finally gave Siri the AI makeover it promised.
  • It can write emails in your tone and rescue badly framed photos, the company says.
  • And yes, Apple has a solution for the Liquid Glass haters.

Apple's products are about to get more AI-ish.

On Monday, the tech giant is releasing its big annual software update. This year's release is centered on the new AI-powered Siri, Apple's big bet that it can keep pace with rival AI assistants.

Apple's iOS 27 works on iPhone 11 models and newer, though the splashiest Apple Intelligence tools require an iPhone 15 Pro or later. iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are also arriving the same day.

Here are the biggest changes coming to your iPhone's brain:

Siri gets an AI facelift — and a new home
Many of the updates revolve around a more powerful Siri.

Apple

For years, Siri has been a shortcut for setting timers or figuring out if iPhone users needed to pack a rain jacket for the day.

Now, Apple says it'll act more like a personal assistant.

"We know there are times when you expect more from Siri," Mike Rockwell, Apple's VP of Siri engineering, said during the company's Worldwide Developers Conference in June. "Siri is now a profoundly more capable assistant that helps you find what you need and gets more done."

The new Siri AI can answer probing questions, hold longer conversations, and use details across several Apple and third-party apps to find what users need, the company says. It can, for example, find a hotel confirmation in an older email, find a recipe a friend texted a while ago, or enter a café WiFi password after taking a picture.

There's also a new stand-alone Siri AI app where users can revisit conversations on other Apple devices, too.

It's the biggest test yet of Apple's AI ambitions. Siri AI is initially available in English and is partially available in Europe.

New parental controls
Apple is offering several new parent-empowering updates.

Anna Barclay/Getty Images

Apple is trying to make its kid-safety tools more useful before a parent has to confiscate the phone.

Parents setting up an iPhone for a child can decide which built-in apps are available from the start. An Ask to Browse feature also makes a child ask permission before visiting a new website. The parent gets the request in Messages and can approve or decline it.

Screen Time gets more granular, with category-based allowances for entertainment, games, and social media, as well as schedules that control which apps are usable at particular times. Parents can compare their child's screen usage with recommendations from clinical and child development experts, Apple says.

The company has redesigned the parent-facing settings, too, promising a clearer dashboard and quicker in-the-moment controls.

AI photo editing
iOS 27 includes several AI-powered photo editing tools.

Apple

Missed the shot? Apple wants to give you a second chance.

There are several new photo editing tools included in the iOS update: Spatial Reframing lets users adjust a photo's camera perspective after the shutter has been released, Extend uses AI to add space around the edges of an image, and the upgraded Clean Up tool helps delete or reframe blurry elements in a photo.

Siri AI will try to write in your voice
Apple's Siri AI wants to write emails in your voice.

Apple

Siri AI wants a spot at the writer's table, too.

Apple says the updated assistant can start a draft or revise copy in the Mail and Messages apps. The writing can draw on how you usually communicate with a particular person, including a user's typical punctuation and tone. The tools can also offer writing suggestions and automatically proofread text as you type, including in many third-party apps.

Your own shortcut
Apple is trying to turn Shortcuts from a power-user playground into something the rest of us might actually open.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Shortcuts has long been one of the iPhone's coolest and least approachable apps. It lets users stitch together actions across apps, but building a simple automation could require working through a lot of menus.

Now, users can describe what they want in plain English, and Shortcuts will create the workflow. Apple's example: "When I'm leaving work, message Pedro I'm on my way with my ETA."

Easing up on the Liquid Glass
Apple's 2025 update included new Liquid Glass visuals. Now, users can turn them down.

Apple

Liquid Glass is getting a dimmer switch.

Last year, Apple introduced an interface setting that made the edges of some icons look glassier. Now, users can edit that update to their liking. iOS 27 lets users tune the effect from "ultraclear" to fully tinted.

Last year's update didn't receive the warmest of embraces…

Faster speeds
Apple says the update will help make a phone perform faster.

illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images

Apple says iOS 27 will speed up everyday tasks: apps can launch up to 30% faster, new Photos library images can load up to 70% faster, and AirDrop transfers can be up to 80% faster.

It should also switch more smoothly between WiFi and cellular networks.

items.title: Sakana AI Researchers Introduce PC-ALM, a Layer-Local Alternative to Backpropagation That Trains 1000-Layer Networks
items.summary: Backpropagation is a global algorithm: a forward pass, then a backward pass, then a weight update, each locked behind the previous one. Brains have no known mechanism for that kind of network-wide phase locking, which is why local-learning alternatives such as predictive coding (PC) keep drawing research interest. Sakana AI researchers propose Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding (PC-ALM) , a variant of PC that keeps every update layer-local yet recovers backprop-aligned credit signals. The research team reports training residual MLPs up to 1000 layers within about 2 percentage points of backprop on MNIST. Is it deployable? Yes, as research code: an MIT-licensed JAX reference implementation runs on CPU and reproduces the paper’s width-depth grid. It is a training method, not a model, and has only been tested on small image benchmarks. Why standard PC stalls in deep, narrow networks PC treats every hidden activation as an optimization variable and penalizes the squared mismatch between each layer’s activation and the prediction arriving from the layer below. Inference is gradient descent on that energy; learning is a Hebbian-like weight step. The catch is that supervision enters at the output and must diffuse through a chain of local compromises. In deep, narrow networks the credit signal fades long before it reaches the input. Innocenti et al. characterized this PC-BP gap as a function of width and depth, and it is worst when width is smaller than depth. What PC-ALM changes PC-ALM starts from the constrained view of training: minimize the supervised loss subject to h i = σ ( W i h i − 1 ) h_i = \sigma(W_i h_{i-1}) at every layer. PC is the quadratic-penalty relaxation of that problem. PC-ALM uses the augmented Lagrangian instead, attaching a Lagrange multiplier λ i ∈ ℝ d i such that dim ( λ i ) = dim ( h i ) \lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_i} \quad \text{such that} \quad \text{dim}(\lambda_i) = \text{dim}(h_i) to each layer constraint while keeping PC’s penalty. Setting λ = 0 recovers PC exactly. Inference alternates 2 local steps: a primal gradient step on the activations, and a dual step λ i ← λ i + α r i \lambda_i \leftarrow \lambda_i + \alpha r_i that accumulates the layer’s prediction error. Completing the square shows each primal step is a standard PC step with the prediction target shifted by − λ i / ρ -\lambda_i/\rho . After T steps the weight update acts on the composite signal λ i + ρ r i \lambda_i + \rho r_i . The research team read this as a PI controller per layer: the prediction error is the proportional term and the multiplier is the integral term. α = 0 gives PC; α = ρ with the inner problem solved exactly gives the classical method of multipliers. Exact backprop gradients in the linear case LeCun observed in 1988 that the Lagrange multipliers of a constrained network equal the backprop adjoints at a KKT point. The team proves that in linear PC networks, under a spectral-radius stability condition, PC-ALM converges to that KKT point: activations return to their forward-pass values while each λ i \lambda_i integrates to the exact BP adjoint. The per-mode stability bound is η h σ i 2 ( 2 ρ + α ) < 4 \eta_h \sigma_i^2 (2\rho + \alpha) < 4 , which reduces to PC’s condition at α = 0. Unlike PC’s monotone gradient flow, PC-ALM’s iteration matrix has complex eigenvalues that produce damped oscillations; α sets their frequency but not their decay rate. Results The research team sweeps residual MLPs with width and depth from 8 to 128 on Fashion-MNIST and MNIST under the mean-field parameterization of Innocenti et al., training for 1 epoch. With an inference budget of T = 2L, PC-ALM matches backprop across every width, depth, and activation (identity, tanh, ReLU), while PC drops sharply in deep, narrow cells. The repo’s reference cell (width 32, depth 32, ReLU, Fashion-MNIST) reports 78.66% test accuracy for BP, 68.13% for PC, and 77.75% for PC-ALM, with gradient cosine to BP rising from 0.604 to 0.909. The research extends the picture: 1000-layer residual MLPs on MNIST (width 32, ReLU, 5 epochs) stay within roughly 2 points of BP, and PC-ALM improves over PC on every benchmark tried, including ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet. && Key Takeaways PC-ALM adds a per-layer Lagrange multiplier to predictive coding; every update stays layer-local. In linear networks the multipliers converge to exact backprop gradients. Matches BP across the 8 to 128 width-depth grid at T = 2L; PC fails in deep, narrow cells. Trains 1000-layer residual MLPs within about 2 points of BP on MNIST. MIT-licensed JAX code reproduces the results on CPU. Check out the Paper , Blog , and GitHub Repo . Backpropagation is a global algorithm: a forward pass, then a backward pass, then a weight update, each locked behind the previous one. Brains have no known mechanism for that kind of network-wide phase locking, which is why local-learning alternatives such as predictive coding (PC) keep drawing research interest. Sakana AI researchers propose Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding (PC-ALM), a variant of PC that keeps every update layer-local yet recovers backprop-aligned credit signals. The research team reports training residual MLPs up to 1000 layers within about 2 percentage points of backprop on MNIST.

Is it deployable? Yes, as research code: an MIT-licensed JAX reference implementation runs on CPU and reproduces the paper’s width-depth grid. It is a training method, not a model, and has only been tested on small image benchmarks.

Why standard PC stalls in deep, narrow networks

PC treats every hidden activation as an optimization variable and penalizes the squared mismatch between each layer’s activation and the prediction arriving from the layer below. Inference is gradient descent on that energy; learning is a Hebbian-like weight step. The catch is that supervision enters at the output and must diffuse through a chain of local compromises. In deep, narrow networks the credit signal fades long before it reaches the input. Innocenti et al. characterized this PC-BP gap as a function of width and depth, and it is worst when width is smaller than depth.

What PC-ALM changes

PC-ALM starts from the constrained view of training: minimize the supervised loss subject to hi=σ(Wihi−1)h_i = \sigma(W_i h_{i-1}) at every layer. PC is the quadratic-penalty relaxation of that problem. PC-ALM uses the augmented Lagrangian instead, attaching a Lagrange multiplier λi∈ℝdisuch thatdim(λi)=dim(hi)\lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_i} \quad \text{such that} \quad \text{dim}(\lambda_i) = \text{dim}(h_i) to each layer constraint while keeping PC’s penalty. Setting λ = 0 recovers PC exactly.

Inference alternates 2 local steps: a primal gradient step on the activations, and a dual step λi←λi+αri\lambda_i \leftarrow \lambda_i + \alpha r_i that accumulates the layer’s prediction error. Completing the square shows each primal step is a standard PC step with the prediction target shifted by −λi/ρ-\lambda_i/\rho. After T steps the weight update acts on the composite signal λi+ρri\lambda_i + \rho r_i. The research team read this as a PI controller per layer: the prediction error is the proportional term and the multiplier is the integral term. α = 0 gives PC; α = ρ with the inner problem solved exactly gives the classical method of multipliers.

Exact backprop gradients in the linear case

LeCun observed in 1988 that the Lagrange multipliers of a constrained network equal the backprop adjoints at a KKT point. The team proves that in linear PC networks, under a spectral-radius stability condition, PC-ALM converges to that KKT point: activations return to their forward-pass values while each λi\lambda_i integrates to the exact BP adjoint. The per-mode stability bound is ηhσi2(2ρ+α)<4\eta_h \sigma_i^2 (2\rho + \alpha) < 4, which reduces to PC’s condition at α = 0. Unlike PC’s monotone gradient flow, PC-ALM’s iteration matrix has complex eigenvalues that produce damped oscillations; α sets their frequency but not their decay rate.

Results

The research team sweeps residual MLPs with width and depth from 8 to 128 on Fashion-MNIST and MNIST under the mean-field parameterization of Innocenti et al., training for 1 epoch. With an inference budget of T = 2L, PC-ALM matches backprop across every width, depth, and activation (identity, tanh, ReLU), while PC drops sharply in deep, narrow cells. The repo’s reference cell (width 32, depth 32, ReLU, Fashion-MNIST) reports 78.66% test accuracy for BP, 68.13% for PC, and 77.75% for PC-ALM, with gradient cosine to BP rising from 0.604 to 0.909.

The research extends the picture: 1000-layer residual MLPs on MNIST (width 32, ReLU, 5 epochs) stay within roughly 2 points of BP, and PC-ALM improves over PC on every benchmark tried, including ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet.

&&

Key Takeaways
  • PC-ALM adds a per-layer Lagrange multiplier to predictive coding; every update stays layer-local.
  • In linear networks the multipliers converge to exact backprop gradients.
  • Matches BP across the 8 to 128 width-depth grid at T = 2L; PC fails in deep, narrow cells.
  • Trains 1000-layer residual MLPs within about 2 points of BP on MNIST.
  • MIT-licensed JAX code reproduces the results on CPU.

items.title: Trump throws out power plant climate pollution rules
items.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency announced its plans today to kill any remaining standards on how much greenhouse gas pollution power plants are allowed to emit in the US. The move will only make electricity dirtier as AI, electric vehicles, and a revival of domestic manufacturing drive up power demand. The EPA's proposal today is a major escalation of President Donald Trump's efforts to promote fossil fuels while making it easier to build out energy-hungry data centers. items.title: Defense Startup Shield AI in Talks for Valuation of at Least $20 Billion
items.summary: Shield AI, a startup building drones and AI-powered software for the military, is in talks to raise new funds at a valuation of at least $20 billion, according to a person with knowledge of the fundraise. The funding round, if it closes, would represent a roughly 60% increase to Shield’s valuation from just five months ago. The planned funding round follows the 11-year-old company’s success winning contracts for its AI software that coordinates drones and aircrafts, called Hivemind, and comes as investors continue to pour money into startups that are building AI-powered weapons and defense systems.

items.title: Trump called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang mid-interview to rip AI doomerism: 'The robots will not be taking over'
items.summary: President Donald Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI doomer predictions aren't grounded in science. At the All-In Summit, Huang also praised AI researcher Jacob Coxon's courage as a whistleblower. President Donald Trump called in during Huang's talk, saying, "The robots will not be taking over." Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got a call from President Donald Trump in the middle of his interview to swat down AI doomer predictions. On Monday at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, Huang's talk was interrupted by a phone call from President Donald Trump, who called AI doomerism "a hoax." "The robots will not be taking over," Trump said via speakerphone, adding that while "we have to be a little bit careful," the US shouldn't stop AI advancement. The debate on AI safety has roiled Silicon Valley, especially after Jacob Coxon , a former Anthropic researcher, announced last week he resigned from the lab, writing on X that the people building AI "believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." During the talk, Huang praised a former Anthropic researcher for speaking out on AI safety and also said the notion that the technology poses an existential threat is unscientific. Weighing in, Huang called AI safety "paramount" and said that the US can still move fast. "America is able to lead — and to do it safely," he said. Huang said Coxon showed "great courage" by coming forward. He also said there's a difference between exposing existing problems within a company and making predictions about the future. "I think the whistleblowing is fine. I think the scientific prediction about the future is less fine because it's not grounded on science, obviously," Huang said. Huang said he doesn't know what Coxon witnessed inside Anthropic and suggested the industry's frontier labs are undergoing a difficult transition from research to engineering organizations. The Nvidia CEO's comments are consistent with his established views. He's previously pushed back on what he's called "science fiction" scenarios that scare people away from investing in technology that could make AI safer. Trump also posted on Truth Social on Monday, saying that he was "breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World." Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Have a tip? Contact this reporter via email at gweiss@businessinsider.com or Signal at @geoffweiss.25. items.title: Instagram wants you to pay for its AI photo-editing filters
items.summary: Meta is making Instagram users (like me) pay for more access to its AI photo-editing tools. Screenshots/Instagram/BI I've got to admit something. Meta's AI tools for editing photos are … pretty good. But! Meta will soon make you pay if you want to edit tons of your photos with AI. The Meta One monthly subscription will unlock additional AI usage and unique perks for its apps. I was having some unfettered fun playing with Instagram's new filters. Then I got hit with a paywall. "Upgrade to Meta One Core to apply more AI effects or wait until tomorrow," a pop-up said on my screen. Curious, I clicked "Upgrade." I was given the option for a free trial of Meta One , a new subscription that unlocks a litany of perks. While Meta unveiled its newest subscriptions in May, the program hasn't yet been widely rolled out in the US. One of my Instagram accounts was part of a test. If I accepted the monthlong trial, I could edit more photos on the app using Meta's AI "effects" it rolled out in July. After dozens of edits tweaking my latest professional headshots to look like they were taken on a disposable camera, or turning iPhone cat photos into higher-quality editorial shots, I wanted more. Meta's AI tools let users tweak and generate various edits to photos within the Instagram app. Would I share all of these on Insta? Probably not. Screenshots/Instagram/BI I swiftly signed up for the Meta One Core tier, which would renew at $7.99 a month. The perks range from additional AI usage to unlocking the "plus" versions of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. Meta One subscribers can "preview" people's stories without actually watching them, use special app icons (like the retro Instagram one), and visually customize Facebook and WhatsApp. There are also tiers for professional accounts that could appeal to content creators. "We're starting with plans that give people who use Meta AI more to work with," Meta's head of product, Naomi Gleit, said in a May video. "More capacity, bigger, more complex requests, and more room to create." This isn't Meta's first attempt to get consumers to pay for a recurring subscription. In 2023, it launched Meta Verified , which charged users a monthly fee to unlock perks like a blue check mark. Now, Meta wants to paywall premium features like AI. Making people pay for more editing tools, like the Effects Instagram promotes in-app, further pushes Meta up against photo-editing rivals like Adobe's Photoshop, VSCO, and emerging apps like the influencer-founded startup Tezza . Business Insider's Sydney Bradley caved and signed up for a Meta One trial. Screenshots/Instagram/BI Filters have always been part of the Instagram experience. After dozens of edits tweaking my latest professional headshots to look like they were taken on a disposable camera, or turning iPhone cat photos into higher-quality editorial shots, I wanted more.
