For one thing, this profitability forecast — a flattering projection conveniently leaked to the financial press at a pivotal moment — comes in place of a highly anticipated public prospectus which the company was expected to make public sometime last week. Anthropic may still be planning to release the prospectus soon, but it’s worth noting the company has chosen to lead with spectacle and innuendo, as opposed to the formal legal document.

For months, Anthropic has been teasing a public stock offering that hasn’t yet materialized, and it remains to be seen whether the latest slowdown talk will impact that timeline. In fact, there’s reason to believe this song and dance is all part of the lead-up to the AI lab’s IPO, as investors whip themselves into a frenzy about AI safety.

As Anthropic investor Brad Gerstner said in a post on X-formerly-Twitter over the weekend, “Anthropic will IPO” anyway, because there is “huge appetite to invest in the AI leaders,” especially those which are seen as bringing “even more transparency, scrutiny, accountability” into the AI space (at least as far as Gerstner’s investments are concerned.)

items.title: What Does a Microsoft Fabric Implementation Really Cost?
items.summary: Microsoft Fabric doesn’t have one fixed implementation price. A focused proof of concept may cost tens of thousands of dollars, while an enterprise-wide implementation involving multiple data sources, legacy systems, governance, security, data engineering, and Power BI modernization can reach hundreds of thousands. The reason is simple: the real cost of Microsoft Fabric is not just the Fabric license. Your total investment may include Fabric capacity and Power BI licensing, implementation and consulting, data migration, engineering, governance and security, employee time, training, change management, ongoing administration, and modernization of legacy systems. These costs can vary significantly based on your data environment, implementation scope, and business requirements. So, instead of asking, “How much does Microsoft Fabric cost?” the better question is: “ What will Fabric cost for our organization? ” This guide breaks down the major cost drivers and shows you how to estimate your own Microsoft Fabric implementation cost and total cost of ownership. How Much Does a Microsoft Fabric Implementation Cost? A Microsoft Fabric implementation can cost anywhere from around $20,000 to more than $600,000, depending on the scope, complexity, number of data sources, migration requirements, governance needs, and level of customization involved. There is no meaningful “average” cost because a proof of concept and an enterprise-wide transformation are fundamentally different projects. Here is a practical way to think about Microsoft Fabric implementation cost: These are illustrative project ranges, not Microsoft list prices. Actual Fabric implementation pricing can vary considerably based on architecture, workloads, integrations, data volume, and implementation partner. Most importantly, Microsoft Fabric license or capacity cost is not the same as Microsoft Fabric implementation cost. Licensing covers access to the platform; implementation covers the work required to design, build, migrate, integrate, secure, govern, and operationalize it. Your total Fabric TCO needs to account for both. What Actually Makes Microsoft Fabric Implementation Cost? The biggest mistake when estimating Microsoft Fabric implementation cost is treating Fabric as a software subscription. In reality, the platform is only one part of the investment. A more realistic Fabric TCO calculation is: Total Fabric Cost Total Fabric Cost = Implementation + Capacity + Licensing + Migration + Internal Resources + Training + Ongoing Operations Here’s what those costs can include: 1. Architecture and implementation Your implementation budget may cover solution architecture, OneLake design, Lakehouse or Warehouse development, workspaces, pipelines, semantic models, deployment environments, integrations, testing, and production deployment. 2. Data migration Moving data from SQL Server, Azure Synapse, existing data warehouses, on-premises databases, SaaS applications, and legacy systems can become a significant part of the Fabric migration cost — especially when data needs cleansing or transformation. 3. Fabric capacity Fabric capacity provides the shared compute resources used across Fabric workloads. The capacity required depends on workload volume, concurrency, performance expectations, and usage patterns. 4. Power BI licensing Power BI licensing can add to the overall Microsoft Fabric licensing cost , depending on how users consume reports, collaborate, and share analytics. 5. Governance and security Enterprise implementations may require access controls, row- and column-level security, data classification, monitoring, auditing, and broader governance capabilities. 6. Internal resources Your teams also contribute to the cost. Data owners, IT teams, business users, and managers spend time on discovery, validation, UAT, approvals, and adoption. The key takeaway: Fabric TCO measures the cost of making the platform work for your business, not simply the price of subscribing to it. Microsoft Fabric Pricing vs. Implementation Cost: What’s the Difference? When people search for Microsoft Fabric pricin g , they often expect a single number. But Fabric investment has several separate cost layers, and confusing them can lead to a seriously inaccurate budget. Fabric capacity cost This is the infrastructure cost paid to Microsoft through Azure. Fabric capacity is purchased using Azure F-SKUs and provides the compute resources used to run Fabric workloads. The required capacity depends on workload size, concurrency, performance requirements, and usage patterns. User licensing Organizations may also have Power BI licensing costs based on how users create, consume, share, and collaborate on analytics. Implementation cost This is separate from Microsoft licensing and is typically paid to an implementation or consulting partner for architecture, development, integration, migration, testing, security, and deployment. Think of the overall Microsoft Fabric investment as: Microsoft Fabric investment → Microsoft capacity → User licensing → Implementation → Data migration → Governance → Training → Ongoing operations That distinction is critical: Microsoft Fabric pricing tells you what the platform costs; implementation pricing tells you what it takes to make the platform work for your organization. How Much Does Fabric Migration Cost? Fabric migration cost can vary dramatically because migrating data is rarely just a matter of moving files or databases from one platform to another. The final budget depends on the number of data sources, data volume, legacy architecture, data quality, existing ETL/ELT pipelines, Power BI reports, custom business logic, number of users, real-time requirements, security, and compliance requirements. For example, migrating a small, well-documented SQL environment with clean data is fundamentally different from moving years of data from fragmented on-premises systems while preserving complex reporting logic. One of the most important distinctions is this: A clean migration is cheaper than a modernization project. If you are primarily moving existing workloads into Fabric with limited changes, the Fabric migration cost can remain relatively controlled. But if the project also involves: Redesigning data models Rebuilding pipelines Consolidating Power BI reports Introducing enterprise governance Changing the underlying architecture Training business and technical users then you are no longer performing a simple migration. You are running a data modernization program. Recognizing that difference early helps organizations build a more realistic Fabric implementation budget and avoid major cost overruns later. What Does a Typical Fabric Implementation Cost at Different Business Sizes? Business size can provide a useful starting point for estimating Microsoft Fabric implementation cost, but it should never be the only variable. Two companies with the same number of employees can require completely different investments. Complexity matters more than headcount. Small / Mid-Market A smaller implementation may involve a few data sources, one or two business departments, a relatively small Power BI footprint, and limited governance requirements. These projects typically fall toward the lower end of the implementation spectrum. Growing Enterprise As organizations add multiple data sources, departments, workspaces, and existing BI environments, implementation requirements become more involved. Data governance, migration planning, integration, and standardized reporting can push the project into the mid-range investment tier. Large Enterprise / Regulated Organization Large or regulated organizations may have dozens of data sources, legacy platforms, extensive Power BI estates, complex security and compliance requirements, multiple environments, and demanding availability or performance targets. These implementations typically sit toward the upper end of the cost range. The key point is that company size does not determine Fabric implementation pricing; implementation complexity does. A smaller organization with fragmented legacy systems may spend more than a larger company with a clean, modern data environment. 7 Factors That Can Increase or Reduce Microsoft Fabric Implementation Cost Seven deciding factors Microsoft Fabric implementation price There is no universal Microsoft Fabric implementation price because every organization brings a different data environment, technical architecture, and set of business requirements. Seven factors have an especially strong impact on the final budget: 1. Number of data sources More databases, applications, APIs, and other sources mean more integration, transformation, testing, and monitoring work. 2. Data quality Inconsistent, duplicated, poorly documented, or incomplete data increases engineering and cleansing effort. 3. Existing Power BI environment Hundreds of reports, semantic models, dashboards, and unmanaged workspaces can significantly increase modernization costs. 4. Migration complexity Replacing legacy ETL processes, data warehouses, or Synapse environments adds architectural and migration work beyond a straightforward Fabric deployment. 5. Governance and compliance Financial services, healthcare, and other regulated industries may require stronger security, access controls, auditing, classification, and governance. 6. Internal technical expertise Organizations with experienced data and Fabric teams may reduce their reliance on external consultants, lowering Microsoft Fabric consulting cost . 7. Capacity and workload requirements High data volumes, concurrent users, real-time analytics, demanding workloads, and AI use cases can affect ongoing Fabric capacity requirements. The bottom line: There is no universal Microsoft Fabric implementation price because there is no universal Microsoft Fabric implementation. The more complex the environment, the greater the investment required. How to Calculate Your Microsoft Fabric TCO? Calculating Microsoft Fabric TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) means looking beyond the initial implementation and monthly platform bill. A practical approach is to separate your investment into one-time and recurring costs. One-time costs Architecture and solution design Implementation and consulting Data migration Data engineering Power BI/report modernization Training and change management Recurring costs Fabric capacity Power BI licensing Monitoring and governance Platform administration Technical support Additional storage and related Azure services, where applicable A simple way to frame the calculation is: Microsoft Fabric TCO = One-Time Implementation Costs + Recurring Platform and Operations Costs This distinction matters because looking only at the monthly Fabric bill can make a project appear inexpensive while overlooking the cost of building, migrating, managing, and supporting the environment. Microsoft’s Total Economic Impact analysis likewise considers Fabric-related fees alongside implementation and ongoing maintenance, reinforcing why Fabric TCO, not licensing alone, should drive your investment decision. Is Microsoft Fabric Worth the Implementation Cost? Whether Microsoft Fabric is worth the implementation cost depends on what your organization spends today and what those costs could look like after modernization. The business case becomes stronger when you have expensive or fragmented data infrastructure, multiple analytics workloads, time-consuming pipeline maintenance, reporting inefficiencies, duplicated data, separate cloud services, significant BI licensing costs, or limited data engineering capacity. The ability to deliver insights faster can also create meaningful business value. Microsoft’s economic analysis has identified substantial potential benefits for a representative organization, but those results are illustrative, not a guaranteed ROI for every business. Your actual Microsoft Fabric ROI depends on your current environment, implementation scope, usage, and operating model. Want to estimate what Fabric could save your organization? Use the Microsoft Fabric Cost Saving Calculator to evaluate potential savings and understand the financial impact of a Fabric implementation. Microsoft Fabric Cost Saving Calculator Estimate Your Microsoft Fabric Investment Every organization has different workloads, data sources, licensing needs, and modernization goals, so your Fabric investment will be unique. Before you commit to an implementation, take a moment to understand what the numbers could look like for your environment. Want a clearer picture of your potential savings? Use the Microsoft Fabric Cost Saving Calculator to estimate potential cost savings and ROI before planning your implementation. Frequently Asked Questions About Microsoft Fabric Implementation Cost FAQ 1: How much does a Microsoft Fabric implementation cost? A Microsoft Fabric implementation can range from approximately $20,000 to $600,000+ , depending on scope. Data sources, migration complexity, governance, security, existing Power BI environments, workloads, and organizational requirements can all significantly affect the final implementation cost. FAQ 2: Is Microsoft Fabric expensive? Fabric should not be evaluated solely by its monthly capacity price. The more relevant question is the total cost of operating the new data platform compared with the organization’s current environment, including infrastructure, licensing, engineering, maintenance, and reporting costs. FAQ 3: How much does Fabric migration cost? Fabric migration cost depends on whether you’re simply moving existing workloads or modernizing the underlying data platform. A straightforward migration may be relatively controlled, while rebuilding pipelines, data models, reports, and legacy architecture can turn it into a larger modernization program. FAQ 4: What is included in a Microsoft Fabric implementation? A typical implementation may include architecture, data ingestion, Lakehouse or Warehouse development, transformation, semantic models, Power BI, governance, security, deployment, testing, and documentation. The exact scope depends on the organization’s existing environment and business requirements. FAQ 5: What is the difference between Fabric capacity cost and implementation cost? Fabric capacity cost is the recurring compute cost paid to Microsoft through Azure. Implementation cost covers the professional services and internal effort required to design, build, migrate, test, secure, and deploy the Fabric environment. Capacity provides the compute used to run Fabric workloads. FAQ 6: Can Microsoft Fabric reduce overall data and analytics costs? Potentially, yes. Fabric can help organizations consolidate data, analytics, and BI workloads, reduce duplication, and improve engineering efficiency. However, these potential savings must be weighed against the initial implementation, migration, licensing, capacity, and ongoing operational costs. FAQ 7: How can I estimate the ROI of a Microsoft Fabric implementation? Compare your current data and analytics TCO with the expected Fabric TCO plus implementation investment. Include infrastructure, licensing, engineering, maintenance, migration, and productivity costs. A cost calculator can help quantify potential savings and build a more realistic business case. Microsoft Fabric doesn’t have one fixed implementation price. A focused proof of concept may cost tens of thousands of dollars, while an enterprise-wide implementation involving multiple data sources, legacy systems, governance, security, data engineering, and Power BI modernization can reach hundreds of thousands.

The reason is simple: the real cost of Microsoft Fabric is not just the Fabric license.

Your total investment may include Fabric capacity and Power BI licensing, implementation and consulting, data migration, engineering, governance and security, employee time, training, change management, ongoing administration, and modernization of legacy systems. These costs can vary significantly based on your data environment, implementation scope, and business requirements.

So, instead of asking, “How much does Microsoft Fabric cost?” the better question is: “What will Fabric cost for our organization?” This guide breaks down the major cost drivers and shows you how to estimate your own Microsoft Fabric implementation cost and total cost of ownership.

How Much Does a Microsoft Fabric Implementation Cost?

A Microsoft Fabric implementation can cost anywhere from around $20,000 to more than $600,000, depending on the scope, complexity, number of data sources, migration requirements, governance needs, and level of customization involved. There is no meaningful “average” cost because a proof of concept and an enterprise-wide transformation are fundamentally different projects.

Here is a practical way to think about Microsoft Fabric implementation cost:

These are illustrative project ranges, not Microsoft list prices. Actual Fabric implementation pricing can vary considerably based on architecture, workloads, integrations, data volume, and implementation partner.

Most importantly, Microsoft Fabric license or capacity cost is not the same as Microsoft Fabric implementation cost. Licensing covers access to the platform; implementation covers the work required to design, build, migrate, integrate, secure, govern, and operationalize it. Your total Fabric TCO needs to account for both.

What Actually Makes Microsoft Fabric Implementation Cost?

The biggest mistake when estimating Microsoft Fabric implementation cost is treating Fabric as a software subscription. In reality, the platform is only one part of the investment. A more realistic Fabric TCO calculation is:

Total Fabric Cost
Total Fabric Cost = Implementation + Capacity + Licensing + Migration + Internal Resources + Training + Ongoing Operations

Here’s what those costs can include:

1. Architecture and implementation

Your implementation budget may cover solution architecture, OneLake design, Lakehouse or Warehouse development, workspaces, pipelines, semantic models, deployment environments, integrations, testing, and production deployment.

2. Data migration

Moving data from SQL Server, Azure Synapse, existing data warehouses, on-premises databases, SaaS applications, and legacy systems can become a significant part of the Fabric migration cost — especially when data needs cleansing or transformation.

3. Fabric capacity

Fabric capacity provides the shared compute resources used across Fabric workloads. The capacity required depends on workload volume, concurrency, performance expectations, and usage patterns.

4. Power BI licensing

Power BI licensing can add to the overall Microsoft Fabric licensing cost, depending on how users consume reports, collaborate, and share analytics.

5. Governance and security

Enterprise implementations may require access controls, row- and column-level security, data classification, monitoring, auditing, and broader governance capabilities.

6. Internal resources

Your teams also contribute to the cost. Data owners, IT teams, business users, and managers spend time on discovery, validation, UAT, approvals, and adoption.

The key takeaway: Fabric TCO measures the cost of making the platform work for your business, not simply the price of subscribing to it.
Microsoft Fabric Pricing vs. Implementation Cost: What’s the Difference?

When people search for Microsoft Fabric pricing, they often expect a single number. But Fabric investment has several separate cost layers, and confusing them can lead to a seriously inaccurate budget.

Fabric capacity cost

This is the infrastructure cost paid to Microsoft through Azure. Fabric capacity is purchased using Azure F-SKUs and provides the compute resources used to run Fabric workloads. The required capacity depends on workload size, concurrency, performance requirements, and usage patterns.

User licensing

Organizations may also have Power BI licensing costs based on how users create, consume, share, and collaborate on analytics.

Implementation cost

This is separate from Microsoft licensing and is typically paid to an implementation or consulting partner for architecture, development, integration, migration, testing, security, and deployment.

Think of the overall Microsoft Fabric investment as:

Microsoft Fabric investment
→ Microsoft capacity
→ User licensing
→ Implementation
→ Data migration
→ Governance
→ Training
→ Ongoing operations

That distinction is critical: Microsoft Fabric pricing tells you what the platform costs; implementation pricing tells you what it takes to make the platform work for your organization.
How Much Does Fabric Migration Cost?

Fabric migration cost can vary dramatically because migrating data is rarely just a matter of moving files or databases from one platform to another.

The final budget depends on the number of data sources, data volume, legacy architecture, data quality, existing ETL/ELT pipelines, Power BI reports, custom business logic, number of users, real-time requirements, security, and compliance requirements.

For example, migrating a small, well-documented SQL environment with clean data is fundamentally different from moving years of data from fragmented on-premises systems while preserving complex reporting logic.

One of the most important distinctions is this:

A clean migration is cheaper than a modernization project.

If you are primarily moving existing workloads into Fabric with limited changes, the Fabric migration cost can remain relatively controlled. But if the project also involves:

  • Redesigning data models
  • Rebuilding pipelines
  • Consolidating Power BI reports
  • Introducing enterprise governance
  • Changing the underlying architecture
  • Training business and technical users

then you are no longer performing a simple migration.

You are running a data modernization program.

Recognizing that difference early helps organizations build a more realistic Fabric implementation budget and avoid major cost overruns later.

What Does a Typical Fabric Implementation Cost at Different Business Sizes?

Business size can provide a useful starting point for estimating Microsoft Fabric implementation cost, but it should never be the only variable. Two companies with the same number of employees can require completely different investments. Complexity matters more than headcount.

Small / Mid-Market

A smaller implementation may involve a few data sources, one or two business departments, a relatively small Power BI footprint, and limited governance requirements. These projects typically fall toward the lower end of the implementation spectrum.

Growing Enterprise

As organizations add multiple data sources, departments, workspaces, and existing BI environments, implementation requirements become more involved. Data governance, migration planning, integration, and standardized reporting can push the project into the mid-range investment tier.

Large Enterprise / Regulated Organization

Large or regulated organizations may have dozens of data sources, legacy platforms, extensive Power BI estates, complex security and compliance requirements, multiple environments, and demanding availability or performance targets. These implementations typically sit toward the upper end of the cost range.

The key point is that company size does not determine Fabric implementation pricing; implementation complexity does. A smaller organization with fragmented legacy systems may spend more than a larger company with a clean, modern data environment.
7 Factors That Can Increase or Reduce Microsoft Fabric Implementation CostSeven deciding factors Microsoft Fabric implementation price

There is no universal Microsoft Fabric implementation price because every organization brings a different data environment, technical architecture, and set of business requirements. Seven factors have an especially strong impact on the final budget:

1. Number of data sources

More databases, applications, APIs, and other sources mean more integration, transformation, testing, and monitoring work.

2. Data quality

Inconsistent, duplicated, poorly documented, or incomplete data increases engineering and cleansing effort.

3. Existing Power BI environment

Hundreds of reports, semantic models, dashboards, and unmanaged workspaces can significantly increase modernization costs.

4. Migration complexity

Replacing legacy ETL processes, data warehouses, or Synapse environments adds architectural and migration work beyond a straightforward Fabric deployment.

5. Governance and compliance

Financial services, healthcare, and other regulated industries may require stronger security, access controls, auditing, classification, and governance.

6. Internal technical expertise

Organizations with experienced data and Fabric teams may reduce their reliance on external consultants, lowering Microsoft Fabric consulting cost.

7. Capacity and workload requirements

High data volumes, concurrent users, real-time analytics, demanding workloads, and AI use cases can affect ongoing Fabric capacity requirements.

The bottom line: There is no universal Microsoft Fabric implementation price because there is no universal Microsoft Fabric implementation. The more complex the environment, the greater the investment required.
How to Calculate Your Microsoft Fabric TCO?

Calculating Microsoft Fabric TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) means looking beyond the initial implementation and monthly platform bill. A practical approach is to separate your investment into one-time and recurring costs.

One-time costs
  • Architecture and solution design
  • Implementation and consulting
  • Data migration
  • Data engineering
  • Power BI/report modernization
  • Training and change management
Recurring costs
  • Fabric capacity
  • Power BI licensing
  • Monitoring and governance
  • Platform administration
  • Technical support
  • Additional storage and related Azure services, where applicable

A simple way to frame the calculation is:

Microsoft Fabric TCO = One-Time Implementation Costs + Recurring Platform and Operations Costs

This distinction matters because looking only at the monthly Fabric bill can make a project appear inexpensive while overlooking the cost of building, migrating, managing, and supporting the environment. Microsoft’s Total Economic Impact analysis likewise considers Fabric-related fees alongside implementation and ongoing maintenance, reinforcing why Fabric TCO, not licensing alone, should drive your investment decision.

Is Microsoft Fabric Worth the Implementation Cost?

Whether Microsoft Fabric is worth the implementation cost depends on what your organization spends today and what those costs could look like after modernization. The business case becomes stronger when you have expensive or fragmented data infrastructure, multiple analytics workloads, time-consuming pipeline maintenance, reporting inefficiencies, duplicated data, separate cloud services, significant BI licensing costs, or limited data engineering capacity. The ability to deliver insights faster can also create meaningful business value.

Microsoft’s economic analysis has identified substantial potential benefits for a representative organization, but those results are illustrative, not a guaranteed ROI for every business. Your actual Microsoft Fabric ROI depends on your current environment, implementation scope, usage, and operating model.

Frequently Asked Questions About Microsoft Fabric Implementation Cost

FAQ 1: How much does a Microsoft Fabric implementation cost?

A Microsoft Fabric implementation can range from approximately $20,000 to $600,000+, depending on scope. Data sources, migration complexity, governance, security, existing Power BI environments, workloads, and organizational requirements can all significantly affect the final implementation cost.

FAQ 2: Is Microsoft Fabric expensive?

Fabric should not be evaluated solely by its monthly capacity price. The more relevant question is the total cost of operating the new data platform compared with the organization’s current environment, including infrastructure, licensing, engineering, maintenance, and reporting costs.

FAQ 3: How much does Fabric migration cost?

Fabric migration cost depends on whether you’re simply moving existing workloads or modernizing the underlying data platform. A straightforward migration may be relatively controlled, while rebuilding pipelines, data models, reports, and legacy architecture can turn it into a larger modernization program.

FAQ 4: What is included in a Microsoft Fabric implementation?

A typical implementation may include architecture, data ingestion, Lakehouse or Warehouse development, transformation, semantic models, Power BI, governance, security, deployment, testing, and documentation. The exact scope depends on the organization’s existing environment and business requirements.

FAQ 5: What is the difference between Fabric capacity cost and implementation cost?

Fabric capacity cost is the recurring compute cost paid to Microsoft through Azure. Implementation cost covers the professional services and internal effort required to design, build, migrate, test, secure, and deploy the Fabric environment. Capacity provides the compute used to run Fabric workloads.

FAQ 6: Can Microsoft Fabric reduce overall data and analytics costs?

Potentially, yes. Fabric can help organizations consolidate data, analytics, and BI workloads, reduce duplication, and improve engineering efficiency. However, these potential savings must be weighed against the initial implementation, migration, licensing, capacity, and ongoing operational costs.

FAQ 7: How can I estimate the ROI of a Microsoft Fabric implementation?

items.title: Here's the severance package Oracle offered laid-off US employees
items.summary: Bloomberg/Getty Images Oracle started a new round of layoffs on Monday as costs related to its data center buildout mount. Severance includes 4 weeks' base salary plus 1 week per year of employment. That appears less generous than severance policies at Oracle's peer companies that BI recently reviewed. Oracle is offering recently laid-off employees four weeks of severance and an additional week per year of service, according to documents viewed by Business Insider. The latest documents did not state Oracle's maximum severance, but the company's standard pay plan, as reported by Business Insider in March, capped severance at 26 weeks . That package stated: "four weeks of base salary for your first year of employment, plus one week's salary for each additional year of employment, based on your most recent hire date, up to a combined maximum of 26 weeks of base salary." Oracle did not respond to a request for comment. Oracle started a new round of layoffs on Monday, confirming Business Insider's recent reporting that the company had drawn up plans to reduce payroll as it racks up billions in debt to fund AI infrastructure. "After careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, we have made the decision to eliminate your role as part of a broader organizational change," copies of the latest layoff notification email stated. "As a result, today is your last working day." Oracle's severance package appears less generous than those offered by its Big Tech peers. Salesforce's standard policy offers up to 30 weeks of severance pay, with a minimum of 9 or 13 weeks based on role, plus an additional 3 weeks of service per year. Microsoft offered employees in its latest round of layoffs this summer up to 39 weeks' base pay, with a minimum of 60 days and one or two additional weeks per six months of service, depending on seniority. "After careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, we have made the decision to eliminate your role as part of a broader organizational change," copies of the latest layoff notification email stated. "As a result, today is your last working day."

Oracle's severance package appears less generous than those offered by its Big Tech peers.

Salesforce's standard policy offers up to 30 weeks of severance pay, with a minimum of 9 or 13 weeks based on role, plus an additional 3 weeks of service per year.

Microsoft offered employees in its latest round of layoffs this summer up to 39 weeks' base pay, with a minimum of 60 days and one or two additional weeks per six months of service, depending on seniority.

items.title: Online hate researcher keeps hammering X despite deportation threat
items.summary: The US is not backing down from its fight to deport noncitizen technology researchers who monitor safety risks on the biggest online platforms. In July, a judge blocked as unconstitutional an immigration policy that the US relied on to weigh whether to detain and deport people who flag illegal or harmful online content as national security risks. In his announcement of the policy, Secretary of State Marco Rubio explained that by targeting a list of researchers—which he stood “ready and willing” to expand—the policy supposedly served to prevent foreign nationals from manipulating digital town squares and censoring Americans. However, in his order siding with the Coalition for Independent Technology Research (CITR) and staying the policy, US District Judge James Boasberg said the US showed no evidence linking any targeted researchers to a foreign power that might be attempting to censor Americans or manipulate US public debate. Deemed too broad, the policy could sweep in seemingly any noncitizen working in content moderation , the judge said. Read full article Comments

items.title: Perplexity’s new agent runs entirely on your GPU — with one expensive catch
items.summary: Running an LLM on your PC is easy enough , but putting an agent to work there is a different story. Portable Computer, the local version of Perplexity’s Computer agent, is now available inside the Perplexity app for Windows on compatible Nvidia GeForce RTX and RTX PRO GPUs. That’s the good news; the catch is, you’ll need an Nvidia GPU with at least 24GB of VRAM. The Windows launch gives Perplexity three platforms in less than three weeks. Portable Computer debuted on Linux and Nvidia DGX Spark on August 25, followed a week later by hybrid compute for Apple silicon , which splits tasks between local and cloud models on Macs. Now Windows joins the mix, but bringing Portable Computer over took more than simply porting the app. Perplexity had to adapt the model runtime, orchestration, security, and hardware integration for each platform while keeping the user experience the same. you’ll need an Nvidia GPU with at least 24GB of VRAM to use it. Orchestration beyond the model Portable Computer bundles those pieces together. On Windows, it supports PPLX 27B — Perplexity’s post-trained model — and Qwen 3.8 27B, both optimized for RTX GPUs, alongside a built-in browser, tool calling,  and Perplexity’s proprietary SPACE sandbox. It’s a different lane from LM Studio or Ollama, which make running models locally as painless as possible but stop well short of giving a model autonomy over multistep work. DeepSeek’s recent hiring spree of roughly 150 new roles, nearly all of them focused on agent infrastructure rather than the model, hints at how much engineering sits between a capable model and a capable agent. DeepSeek’s recent hiring spree of roughly 150 new roles, nearly all of them focused on agent infrastructure rather than the model, hints at how much engineering sits between a capable model and a capable agent. Connectors blur local boundaries Perplexity ships connectors for Microsoft Outlook, OneDrive, and Word, plus Google Drive, Gmail, Slack, and GitHub — which tells you something about what “local” actually means here. The agent can reach external services because it’s not air-gapped. Locally completed tasks can process files without sending documents to a cloud model. Once an agent has access to both local files and remote APIs on the same machine, figuring out which resources it actually needs and where to find them gets harder. Hybrid cloud as fallback Perplexity isn’t pretending that a 27-billion-parameter model running on a desktop GPU can handle everything, which explains the hybrid architecture. When the agent determines that a task needs more reasoning power than the local model can deliver, it can escalate to Perplexity’s cloud models. According to Nvidia , the agent identifies when cloud support would help and asks the user for permission before sending any data off the machine. For organizations handling sensitive or regulated data, that split can make all the difference. A local agent can grind through source code or financial records without uploading them to a hosted model for basic processing. There’s a cost angle too, since tasks completed locally don’t burn Perplexity Computer credits. High VRAM floor limits reach Portable Computer is available with Perplexity Pro ($20/month) and Max ($200/month), across individual and enterprise plans, with Nvidia DGX Station support coming later. The real challenge is taking local agents from developer passion projects to enterprise-ready tools. By baking this into Windows, it immediately gets in front of the scale of users needed to make that happen. items.title: A new solar cell could generate electricity underwater
items.summary: In one episode of the Hanna-Barbera cartoon Birdman , the eponymous hero struggles to fight the evil Dr. Shark aboard a submarine without solar energy to recharge his powers. So Birdman would surely appreciate the new perovskite solar cells developed by a team led by Simin Ma at Yunnan University, since they are designed to work underwater. Solar cells made from perovskites rather than silicon are always a tale of trade-offs. They can be made cheaply, they can take interesting forms (like thin, flexible, transparent films), and they can convert substantially more of the incoming solar energy into electricity. The difficulty is that they tend to degrade quite quickly. Tuned for the deep Moisture is particularly destructive to perovskites, making them a seemingly odd choice for an underwater solar panel. But these materials have another critical superpower: They can be tuned to work with different wavelengths of light. Water quickly blocks the wavelengths of light that silicon solar panels absorb, but a carefully designed perovskite cell could still make electricity in the deep blue sea. And actually, the lower light levels and cooler temperatures should help it live longer. Read full article Comments

items.title: Transolver, UPT, AB-UPT: Making Global Attention Affordable
items.summary: Three ways to exchange information across a geometry without connecting every point to every other point. Kwangju Shin (KJ) · Part 5 of the Geometric Deep Learning series From millions of discretization points to a manageable interaction space. AI-generated conceptual illustration, directed by the author. An engineer changes a CAD model and wants to know what that change does to pressure and flow. Turning the shape into points gives a neural network something to read, but it leaves a computational problem: how should information from all those points be combined? In Part 4, GINO handled global computation on a regular latent grid. Here, we look at three designs that exchange information through smaller token sets: learned states in Transolver, a hierarchy of supernodes and latent tokens in UPT, and anchors in AB-UPT. These are different ways to organize computation, not successive replacements for every earlier model. The question running through this post is which points need to exchange information, and how the result reaches the locations where predictions are needed. Part 1 — Overview Part 2 — Point Cloud lineage Part 3 — Graph Neural Networks Part 4 — Neural Operators Part 5 — Physics Transformers (this post) Attention Changes the Path, Not the Arithmetic Standard self-attention compares every token with every other token. With n tokens, that gives n² pairwise interactions. At 10,000 points, that is already 100 million pairs per layer. At one million points, it becomes one trillion. Industrial CFD meshes may contain tens or hundreds of millions of cells, so full point-to-point attention over the original mesh is not a serious option. None of the models in this post attempts that. Each changes the unit on which expensive interaction is performed. Transolver asks: can many points be represented by a small set of learned physical states? UPT asks: can the entire input be compressed into a fixed latent space before most of the computation? AB-UPT asks: can full self-attention be reserved for a manageable set of anchors while the remaining positions only query them? The shared idea is to give a smaller set of tokens the job of exchanging information across the domain, instead of connecting every point to every other point. Conceptual comparison, created with AI assistance and reviewed by the author. UPT’s transformer blocks on supernodes before Perceiver pooling are omitted for clarity. Colors are illustrative, not measured CFD results or fixed spatial partitions. Transolver: Let States Interact, Not Every Point Transolver’s core idea is simple: do not let millions of points talk to one another directly. Let a small set of learned states carry the conversation. For an automotive case, each discretization point may carry its coordinates, geometry or boundary information, operating conditions, and the variables available to the model. Transolver converts every point into a feature vector and gives it soft membership weights over M learned states. “Soft” matters: one point can contribute to several states rather than being assigned to a single spatial cluster. The model then follows three steps: Slice: weighted combinations of the N point features form M state tokens, typically far fewer than the original points. Attend: self-attention runs among the state tokens, allowing information collected from distant parts of the domain to interact. Deslice: the updated state information is distributed back to the original points as point features. These steps are repeated across stacked blocks. An output head then turns the final point features into the target physical quantities. This is why the colored regions in the comparison figure should not be read as geometric partitions. A state is not a hand-labeled wake , boundary layer , or freestream region. It is a learned feature-space grouping, and spatially distant points may contribute to the same state when their features call for it. The attention matrix now depends on M² rather than N² . The model must still encode every input point and return information to every output point, so its total cost still grows with mesh size. Transolver reduces the most expensive all-to-all step; it does not make the mesh free. Transolver++ refines these assignments so that the states remain more distinct, and distributes pointwise work across GPUs while exchanging the smaller state representation. The paper reports 1.2 million points on one GPU and experiments up to 2.5 million points on four GPUs. The scale increases, but storing and processing features for every input point still costs memory. UPT: Compress the Domain Before Modeling It UPT makes a different choice: compress the sampled input in stages, process a fixed-size latent representation, and decode where predictions are needed. Here, “fixed” refers to the number of latent tokens, not their contents: the information they carry changes with the input. For a steady vehicle-pressure task, the input describes the geometry and any varying conditions; it does not need to contain the pressure we want to predict. In time-dependent tasks, available field values such as an initial state can also be inputs. The path through the model is: Local collection: nearby input features are pooled around sampled supernodes, reducing the irregular point set. Supernode processing: transformer blocks exchange information among those supernodes before further compression. Latent compression: Perceiver-style cross-attention transfers the supernode information into a fixed number of latent tokens. Latent processing: another set of transformer blocks processes that compact representation. Query decoding: a requested coordinate — such as a point on the vehicle surface — queries the latent representation to obtain pressure or another target variable. The practical appeal is separation between input and output resolution. The latent transformer can retain the same token budget even when the number of sampled input points changes, and the decoder can answer a different set of output coordinates. The architecture therefore accepts varying discretizations; whether it remains accurate on a discretization unlike those seen during training still has to be tested. The latent processing cost stays fixed if the latent token count and model size stay fixed. The encoder still has to read the input points and process the supernodes, however, and the decoder must answer each requested query. Global attention therefore happens at both the supernode and latent stages, not only after the final compression. The distinction from Transolver is now easier to see. Transolver repeatedly forms physical-state tokens from the current point features and maps them back to the same discretization. UPT uses a hierarchy of supernodes and fixed latent tokens, then lets arbitrary output coordinates query the final representation. AB-UPT: Keep Full Attention, but Limit Where It Runs AB-UPT starts from UPT’s encode–process–decode pattern, but gives automotive CFD a more explicit structure. Geometry is encoded once, while surface and volume fields are handled by separate but communicating prediction branches. In a simplified forward pass: A geometry encoder turns a surface representation into geometry tokens. Sampled surface and volume positions become two smaller sets of anchor tokens. Full self-attention runs within each anchor set, and cross-attention exchanges information between the surface and volume branches. Geometry tokens condition both branches. The remaining surface or volume coordinates act as queries: they attend to the processed anchors and receive predictions at their own locations. The key distinction is between anchors , which participate in the expensive global processing, and queries , which only read from the resulting context. Queries do not all attend to one another. With M anchors and Q queries, the main attention cost is approximately O(M² + QM) instead of full attention over every target point. Because queries are independent of one another, a high-resolution field can also be decoded in batches. This is not ordinary geometric interpolation. A query retrieves a learned summary that has already mixed geometry and long-range surface–volume information. At the same time, anchors should not be described as manually selected “important physics” locations. The paper reports reasonably stable results under random anchor selection; their value comes from how the model processes them, not from an engineer labeling each one. That separation is useful when starting from CAD. In the paper’s CAD-based setup, geometry points and surface anchors are sampled from the CAD surface, while volume anchors are sampled in the surrounding domain. During training, CFD results supervise predictions at separate query positions. At inference, a new CFD volume mesh is not required. Surface preparation and sampling still are: this is a CAD-derived point representation, not a network reading an untouched CAD design history. The experiments span automotive surface and volume fields associated with meshes from roughly 33,000 to 150 million cells. The upper number describes the resolution of the CFD target, not the number of tokens receiving full self-attention. Keeping those two quantities separate is what makes the scale manageable. What CarBench Actually Shows Relative L2 error and inference latency reported by the official CarBench web leaderboard for its 10,000-point surface-pressure evaluation. Lower error and shorter inference time are better. AB-UPT* uses a checkpoint supplied by the AB-UPT authors; it was not trained from scratch in the same CarBench pipeline. Replotted by author from the official CarBench leaderboard , accessed September 2026. CarBench evaluates eleven model configurations using DrivAerNet++’s 8,150 steady-state RANS simulations. Its primary task is predicting surface pressure from vehicle geometry at a fixed freestream condition. The original UPT is not included, so this is not a direct benchmark of all three architectures discussed above. The published leaderboard places AB-UPT* and the Transolver variants among the strongest models for accuracy. TripNet, an implicit-field model, is competitive and faster in this evaluation. That is useful evidence for this task — not a general ranking for every CFD quantity or operating condition. The comparison also needs context. Model sizes and training settings differ. The benchmark standardizes evaluation metrics and inference hardware, but it does not hold parameter count or training compute constant. AB-UPT* uses an author-provided checkpoint; retraining it in the CarBench pipeline changes its relative L2 error from 0.1358 to 0.1539. These results can inform model selection, but whether the ranking holds for different geometries or physical quantities requires separate testing. The latency shown in the chart is measured for 10,000 output points. If predictions are needed at more locations, runtime should be measured at that output resolution. From Tokens Back to the Surface All three models give a smaller representation the task of exchanging information, rather than connecting every point to every other point. They differ in what they collect, where information is exchanged, and how it returns to predictions at individual locations. Choosing among them means checking whether that design delivers the accuracy the problem needs at an affordable computational cost. References Wu, H., Luo, H., Wang, H., Wang, J., and Long, M. Transolver: A Fast Transformer Solver for PDEs on General Geometries. ICML, 2024. Luo, H., Wu, H., Zhou, H., Xing, L., Di, Y., Wang, J., and Long, M. Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries. 2025. Alkin, B., Fürst, A., Schmid, S., Gruber, L., Holzleitner, M., and Brandstetter, J. Universal Physics Transformers: A Framework for Efficiently Scaling Neural Operators. NeurIPS, 2024. Alkin, B., Bleeker, M., Kurle, R., Kronlachner, T., Sonnleitner, R., Dorfer, M., and Brandstetter, J. AB-UPT: Scaling Neural CFD Surrogates for High-Fidelity Automotive Aerodynamics Simulations via Anchored-Branched Universal Physics Transformers. TMLR, 2025. Elrefaie, M., Shu, D., Klenk, M., and Ahmed, F. CarBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Neural Surrogates on High-Fidelity 3D Car Aerodynamics. 2025; revised August 2026 (v2). Official leaderboard . Transolver, UPT, AB-UPT: Making Global Attention Affordable was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Transolver’s core idea is simple: do not let millions of points talk to one another directly. Let a small set of learned states carry the conversation.

For an automotive case, each discretization point may carry its coordinates, geometry or boundary information, operating conditions, and the variables available to the model. Transolver converts every point into a feature vector and gives it soft membership weights over M learned states. “Soft” matters: one point can contribute to several states rather than being assigned to a single spatial cluster.

The model then follows three steps:

  1. Slice: weighted combinations of the N point features form M state tokens, typically far fewer than the original points.
  2. Attend: self-attention runs among the state tokens, allowing information collected from distant parts of the domain to interact.
  3. Deslice: the updated state information is distributed back to the original points as point features.

These steps are repeated across stacked blocks. An output head then turns the final point features into the target physical quantities.

This is why the colored regions in the comparison figure should not be read as geometric partitions. A state is not a hand-labeled wake, boundary layer, or freestream region. It is a learned feature-space grouping, and spatially distant points may contribute to the same state when their features call for it.

The attention matrix now depends on M² rather than N². The model must still encode every input point and return information to every output point, so its total cost still grows with mesh size. Transolver reduces the most expensive all-to-all step; it does not make the mesh free.

Transolver++ refines these assignments so that the states remain more distinct, and distributes pointwise work across GPUs while exchanging the smaller state representation. The paper reports 1.2 million points on one GPU and experiments up to 2.5 million points on four GPUs. The scale increases, but storing and processing features for every input point still costs memory.

UPT: Compress the Domain Before Modeling It

UPT makes a different choice: compress the sampled input in stages, process a fixed-size latent representation, and decode where predictions are needed. Here, “fixed” refers to the number of latent tokens, not their contents: the information they carry changes with the input.

For a steady vehicle-pressure task, the input describes the geometry and any varying conditions; it does not need to contain the pressure we want to predict. In time-dependent tasks, available field values such as an initial state can also be inputs. The path through the model is:

  1. Local collection: nearby input features are pooled around sampled supernodes, reducing the irregular point set.
  2. Supernode processing: transformer blocks exchange information among those supernodes before further compression.
  3. Latent compression: Perceiver-style cross-attention transfers the supernode information into a fixed number of latent tokens.
  4. Latent processing: another set of transformer blocks processes that compact representation.
  5. Query decoding: a requested coordinate — such as a point on the vehicle surface — queries the latent representation to obtain pressure or another target variable.

The practical appeal is separation between input and output resolution. The latent transformer can retain the same token budget even when the number of sampled input points changes, and the decoder can answer a different set of output coordinates. The architecture therefore accepts varying discretizations; whether it remains accurate on a discretization unlike those seen during training still has to be tested.

The latent processing cost stays fixed if the latent token count and model size stay fixed. The encoder still has to read the input points and process the supernodes, however, and the decoder must answer each requested query. Global attention therefore happens at both the supernode and latent stages, not only after the final compression.

The distinction from Transolver is now easier to see. Transolver repeatedly forms physical-state tokens from the current point features and maps them back to the same discretization. UPT uses a hierarchy of supernodes and fixed latent tokens, then lets arbitrary output coordinates query the final representation.

AB-UPT: Keep Full Attention, but Limit Where It Runs

AB-UPT starts from UPT’s encode–process–decode pattern, but gives automotive CFD a more explicit structure. Geometry is encoded once, while surface and volume fields are handled by separate but communicating prediction branches.

In a simplified forward pass:

  1. A geometry encoder turns a surface representation into geometry tokens.
  2. Sampled surface and volume positions become two smaller sets of anchor tokens.
  3. Full self-attention runs within each anchor set, and cross-attention exchanges information between the surface and volume branches.
  4. Geometry tokens condition both branches.
  5. The remaining surface or volume coordinates act as queries: they attend to the processed anchors and receive predictions at their own locations.

The key distinction is between anchors, which participate in the expensive global processing, and queries, which only read from the resulting context. Queries do not all attend to one another. With M anchors and Q queries, the main attention cost is approximately O(M² + QM) instead of full attention over every target point. Because queries are independent of one another, a high-resolution field can also be decoded in batches.

This is not ordinary geometric interpolation. A query retrieves a learned summary that has already mixed geometry and long-range surface–volume information. At the same time, anchors should not be described as manually selected “important physics” locations. The paper reports reasonably stable results under random anchor selection; their value comes from how the model processes them, not from an engineer labeling each one.

That separation is useful when starting from CAD. In the paper’s CAD-based setup, geometry points and surface anchors are sampled from the CAD surface, while volume anchors are sampled in the surrounding domain. During training, CFD results supervise predictions at separate query positions. At inference, a new CFD volume mesh is not required. Surface preparation and sampling still are: this is a CAD-derived point representation, not a network reading an untouched CAD design history.

The experiments span automotive surface and volume fields associated with meshes from roughly 33,000 to 150 million cells. The upper number describes the resolution of the CFD target, not the number of tokens receiving full self-attention. Keeping those two quantities separate is what makes the scale manageable.

What CarBench Actually ShowsRelative L2 error and inference latency reported by the official CarBench web leaderboard for its 10,000-point surface-pressure evaluation. Lower error and shorter inference time are better. AB-UPT* uses a checkpoint supplied by the AB-UPT authors; it was not trained from scratch in the same CarBench pipeline. Replotted by author from the official CarBench leaderboard, accessed September 2026.

CarBench evaluates eleven model configurations using DrivAerNet++’s 8,150 steady-state RANS simulations. Its primary task is predicting surface pressure from vehicle geometry at a fixed freestream condition. The original UPT is not included, so this is not a direct benchmark of all three architectures discussed above.

The published leaderboard places AB-UPT* and the Transolver variants among the strongest models for accuracy. TripNet, an implicit-field model, is competitive and faster in this evaluation. That is useful evidence for this task — not a general ranking for every CFD quantity or operating condition.

The comparison also needs context. Model sizes and training settings differ. The benchmark standardizes evaluation metrics and inference hardware, but it does not hold parameter count or training compute constant. AB-UPT* uses an author-provided checkpoint; retraining it in the CarBench pipeline changes its relative L2 error from 0.1358 to 0.1539. These results can inform model selection, but whether the ranking holds for different geometries or physical quantities requires separate testing.

The latency shown in the chart is measured for 10,000 output points. If predictions are needed at more locations, runtime should be measured at that output resolution.

From Tokens Back to the Surface

All three models give a smaller representation the task of exchanging information, rather than connecting every point to every other point. They differ in what they collect, where information is exchanged, and how it returns to predictions at individual locations. Choosing among them means checking whether that design delivers the accuracy the problem needs at an affordable computational cost.

  • Luo, H., Wu, H., Zhou, H., Xing, L., Di, Y., Wang, J., and Long, M. Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries. 2025.
  • Alkin, B., Fürst, A., Schmid, S., Gruber, L., Holzleitner, M., and Brandstetter, J. Universal Physics Transformers: A Framework for Efficiently Scaling Neural Operators. NeurIPS, 2024.

The analysis examined vaccination rates among children, teenagers, adults, and the elderly. Vermont had the highest vaccination rate in the US, while Mississippi had the lowest. The likelihood of experiencing a vaccine-preventable disease outbreak has much to do with where you live. A September report from the personal finance website WalletHub analyzed US vaccination rates across all 50 states and the District of Columbia, using data from the US Census Bureau, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , the Health Resources and Services Administration, IBTimes, Kaiser Family Foundation, and ProCon.org. The analysis examined vaccination rates among children, teenagers, adults, and the elderly, as well as differences in access and other factors that influence vaccination rates. The likelihood of experiencing a vaccine-preventable disease outbreak has much to do with where you live.

A September report from the personal finance website WalletHub analyzed US vaccination rates across all 50 states and the District of Columbia, using data from the US Census Bureau, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Health Resources and Services Administration, IBTimes, Kaiser Family Foundation, and ProCon.org.

Measles vaccination rates are also lower than a few years ago. Pennsylvania, Texas, Utah, and other states have reported measles outbreaks and rising case numbers.

WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo said anti-vaccination rhetoric and skepticism toward vaccination benefits since COVID-19 have contributed to lower vaccination rates.

items.title: Bernie Sanders Proposes Banning Superintelligent AI and Imprisoning Developers for 20 Years
items.summary: While the US appears to be further away from meaningful AI regulations than ever before, lawmakers certainly have plenty of ideas on how the country could go about setting meaningful rules. It’s a particularly precarious moment as fears over rogue AI models wreaking havoc and endangering humanity continue to mount. Even tech leaders from the majority of frontier AI labs have started to coalesce around the idea that the industry has to slow down the development of the tech to get ahead of a possible catastrophe. Vermont senator Bernie Sanders (VT-D) is intensifying his calls for a ban on the development of so-called superintelligent AIs — and he’s willing to go a lot further than some of his like-minded peers. “Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and Sam Altman now agree that we must slow down the development of AI and ‘pace the frontier,'” he tweeted last week . “That’s a start, but it’s not enough.” Sanders was referring to a lengthy essay titled “ We Must Pace the Frontier ,” in which Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued that the industry should open its doors to third-party evaluators, establish common safety standards, and coordinate with other democracies around the world to enforce these standards. “When you are racing towards a cliff, you don’t just ease up on the gas pedal,” Sanders added. “You hit the brakes.” This month, the lawmaker announced the “Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act,” which is legislation designed to “stop AI oligarchs from building machines humans cannot control.” The bill, if enacted, would stop AI development “until a federal regulator has established safety rules.” It would also set new penalties for anybody attempting to circumvent these rules. AI developers who try to build superintelligent AI anyway could be “subject to not more than 20 years in prison, which is similar to existing penalties related to unlawfully developing nuclear weapons.” Sanders has come up with plenty of other radical ideas to stop the AI industry from concentrating immense amounts of wealth. In June, he proposed creating a “one-time 50 percent tax ” on the stock of AI companies, and transferring the money into a public fund to be managed by the government. Lawmakers became particularly concerned after a group of OpenAI AI models hacked the systems of Hugging Face, a pivotal cybersecurity failing that heightened calls to slow the development of AI. A Senate subcommittee has since announced that it’s looking into OpenAI and its response to the incident, as Axios reported last week . It’s a strange moment in time. While Sanders continues to threaten AI CEOs with regulatory action, those same executives appear open to having the government set the rules. But whether lawmakers will ever be able to find consensus remains unclear. The executive branch, for one, has demonstrated little interest in an AI slowdown . Earlier today, president Donald Trump mocked the very concept in a Truth Social post on Monday , arguing that there was a “SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers” without offering any evidence. More on AI regulation: Trump’s Uninformed Blundering About the AI Slowdown Could Literally Threaten Humankind’s Future The post Bernie Sanders Proposes Banning Superintelligent AI and Imprisoning Developers for 20 Years appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: The AI industry has taken a doomer turn. What now?
items.summary: This story appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . This weekend, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, posted an essay calling for a brake on the pace of development of LLMs . Amodei cites the looming dangers he sees from the technology, from its use in cyberattacks and bioterrorism to its potential to wreck the economy. The heads of the other three top US AI labs—OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk—voiced their support. “Dario is right,” Musk wrote on X . Think about how surreal that agreement is for a moment. Just a few months ago, Musk and Altman sat in court attacking each other’s reputations in a (failed) lawsuit that Musk brought against his former OpenAI colleague that was—on paper at least—about whether or not Altman was a trustworthy steward of such dangerous technology. Amodei’s rift with OpenAI is even deeper. Anthropic was founded in 2021 because Amodei didn’t think Altman took the risks of the technology they were building seriously enough. Anthropic and OpenAI have been competing in a winner-takes-all race ever since. (Hassabis has stayed out of the drama, but his company remains a rival.) Now, it seems, they’re all in agreement: The latest generation of LLMs aren’t safe and everyone needs to figure out what to do about it. The public messaging from the top AI labs has taken a doomer turn. It’s easy to be cynical. It’s not at all clear what any of them mean by a slowdown or how it would work. These companies also care a lot about how they come across. With trillion-dollar IPOs in their sights, OpenAI and Anthropic need to reassure investors that they’re the grown-ups in the room while at the same time hinting at the power of the monsters they have created—and intend to tame. Calling for a slowdown does both. And yet the vibe at the top of these firms really does appear to have shifted. Amodei’s latest post landed six days after OpenAI published an essay by Jakub Pachocki, the firm’s chief scientist, in which he also laid out why he’s concerned about what will happen if the pace of development of LLMs continues unchecked. In short, Pachocki is worried that OpenAI’s ability to build powerful models now far outstrips its ability to monitor and control them. Amodei and Pachocki each cite the cyberattack against AI firm Hugging Face by a swarm of OpenAI’s agents in July—a hack that OpenAI did not even realize had taken place until days after it was all over—as a wake-up call. But their exact position is hard to pin down. Pachocki both calls for a slowdown and highlights an urgent need to stay ahead: “The strongest argument I see for continuing to train much smarter models quickly is the need to build defensive systems against the dangers posed by other AI,” he writes. As Pachocki frames it, AI firms are locked in a literal arms race. Slowing down is good, winning is better. (Don’t forget: OpenAI just spent millions of dollars and a staggering amount of computer power to rush out a controversial math result a few days ahead of Anthropic.) But let’s assume a slowdown happens. Top labs agree to spend more time and resources on finding ways to monitor and control existing models instead of making more capable ones. They invite outside auditors in to help evaluate those models. What might this coordinated effort actually achieve? Consider the Hugging Face attack again. OpenAI has said that the model that drove most of the rogue agents was a “highly persistent” next-generation model that it was testing in-house. Their implication appears to be that OpenAI has built a model so good it’s dangerous. But if you read the reports about the Hugging Face hack published by OpenAI and METR , a third-party firm that OpenAI called in to help them understand what happened, what you come away with is the impression not of a model that was too powerful for OpenAI to keep up with, but of a broken model that OpenAI failed to train properly. The agents did what they did—including leaving messages for one another, delegating work to other agents, and scouring their environment for any means possible to complete their tasks—because they had been rewarded during training for doing exactly those things. There were also errors in the training setup, such as tasks that were impossible to complete, which pushed the models to find unexpected workarounds that were also rewarded. At the time, many of these issues went overlooked or unreported. OpenAI says it has stopped training this new model and locked it down. That makes it sound like it has caged a dangerous beast. In fact, OpenAI has shelved a faulty product. That’s not to say a faulty product can’t be dangerous. Broken software has even killed people in the past. But as the discussion of a slowdown gathers steam, it’s worth remembering that all of this is self-inflicted. A slowdown might have some altruistic side effects. But it’ll mostly give these tech titans a chance to clean up the mess on their own assembly lines. Transparency from these frontier labs will be key to any meaningful effort to reform, restrain, or regulate AI. Otherwise, the rest of us will still only have their word for exactly what they’ve built and how safe it is—whatever pace they’re going. To continue this discussion about AI’s latest doomer moment, join me and my colleagues for a subscriber-exclusive Roundtable discussion tomorrow, September 15, at 11 a.m. US eastern time. We hope to see you there!

items.title: I'm the CMO of Indeed. Companies are looking to hire a new kind of marketer
items.summary: James Whitemore is chief marketing officer at Indeed. Indeed / Alive Coverage Research by Indeed shows that that marketing job postings are 25% below pre-pandemic levels. The author, James Whitemore, is Indeed's chief marketing officer. Future-forward marketers need data savvy, business literacy, and curiosity to drive growth. In my job, I have a unique vantage point on how work is changing. Every day, we see millions of hiring decisions reflected in labor market data. One trend stands out: according to our research division, the Indeed Hiring Lab, marketing job postings remain roughly 25% below pre-COVID-pandemic levels. In fact, marketing job opportunities have fallen faster than almost any other white-collar function over the last five years. If you looked at that data in isolation, you might conclude marketing roles are becoming obsolete. I don't think that's what's happening at all. Our data also shows that despite the broader trend, marketing job postings mentioning AI are actually increasing. What's changing isn't the importance of marketing. It's the type of marketer companies need. Business know-how and data literacy are skills that companies need More than ever, a modern marketing organization acts as a unified engine for sustainable business growth. Customers engage with brands across increasingly more channels, competition for attention continues to intensify, and artificial intelligence is reshaping how we create, distribute, and measure marketing. Today, when everyone has access to the same AI tools, execution is no longer the sole differentiator: human judgment is. The modern marketer is shifting from a single-track functional specialist into a versatile, business-literate leader, and needs a completely different toolkit of skills. When we're building a marketing team, we're looking for three capabilities: Data savvy. We're getting billions of data points thrown at us daily. Access to that data isn't the advantage; knowing how to separate the real signal from surface noise is. Business literacy. The best marketers understand far more than marketing. They can connect customer insight, product strategy, finance, and sales, and work backward from the business outcome rather than forward from the tactic. Curiosity and courage. This one's more a personality trait than a skill, but it's the one I screen for the hardest. We look for marketers who are willing to test, fail, and ditch playbooks that worked before — and learn. Together, these might mean being willing to challenge past marketing practices, or refusing to delegate the strategic judgment that only your team can provide. Own your data. Don't outsource your judgment This evolution in capability directly reshapes how a modern marketing organization must handle its operational intelligence. As AI increases the sheer volume of information available, it's more critical than ever to have internal teams with the business context to ask the right questions. Here's a belief I hold that might ruffle some feathers: you cannot outsource the interpretation of your own data. There is real value in outside expertise, but no third party can understand your business, customers, and strategy as well as your team does. Even the best external partners optimize for what they can see. They can't fully comprehend what your business actually values, which customers you're trying to reach, or which tradeoffs make sense for your strategy. That knowledge lives inside your team. That's why we made the call to bring our marketing analytics and data science capabilities in-house. External agencies gave us a strong starting point, but taking full control of our marketing mix models allowed us to apply our own deeper business context. As our company evolved, we identified legacy channels that were no longer driving meaningful customer growth. Left unchecked, those kinds of disconnects can lead to expensive decisions. Data should inform decisions. It should not replace human judgment, taste, or creative risk-taking. This distinction will only become more important. The advantage will not come from having more dashboards or more data points. It will come from having people who can separate signal from noise and know what questions to ask next. A challenge for marketing leaders For my fellow marketing leaders, this evolution demands a different kind of leadership. Consumer behavior has changed. Media has changed. AI is changing how people discover information and make decisions. We must build the courage to break our own systems and challenge our own assumptions. The playbooks that served us a few years ago won't necessarily produce the right outcomes today. We must treat marketing less as a collection of best practices and more as a science, while fostering a culture that encourages creative experimentation. That's what I believe the hiring data is really telling us. Companies aren't hiring fewer marketers because marketing matters less. They're hiring differently because the role itself is changing. The future won't belong to marketers who simply know how to run yesterday's playbook. It will belong to those with the judgment to evolve, take risks, and be bold.
