items.summary_html:
James Whitemore is chief marketing officer at Indeed.

Indeed / Alive Coverage

  • Research by Indeed shows that that marketing job postings are 25% below pre-pandemic levels.
  • The author, James Whitemore, is Indeed's chief marketing officer.
  • Future-forward marketers need data savvy, business literacy, and curiosity to drive growth.

In my job, I have a unique vantage point on how work is changing. Every day, we see millions of hiring decisions reflected in labor market data.

One trend stands out: according to our research division, the Indeed Hiring Lab, marketing job postings remain roughly 25% below pre-COVID-pandemic levels. In fact, marketing job opportunities have fallen faster than almost any other white-collar function over the last five years.

If you looked at that data in isolation, you might conclude marketing roles are becoming obsolete. I don't think that's what's happening at all. Our data also shows that despite the broader trend, marketing job postings mentioning AI are actually increasing.

What's changing isn't the importance of marketing. It's the type of marketer companies need.

Business know-how and data literacy are skills that companies need

More than ever, a modern marketing organization acts as a unified engine for sustainable business growth. Customers engage with brands across increasingly more channels, competition for attention continues to intensify, and artificial intelligence is reshaping how we create, distribute, and measure marketing.

Today, when everyone has access to the same AI tools, execution is no longer the sole differentiator: human judgment is. The modern marketer is shifting from a single-track functional specialist into a versatile, business-literate leader, and needs a completely different toolkit of skills.

When we're building a marketing team, we're looking for three capabilities:

  • Data savvy. We're getting billions of data points thrown at us daily. Access to that data isn't the advantage; knowing how to separate the real signal from surface noise is.
  • Business literacy. The best marketers understand far more than marketing. They can connect customer insight, product strategy, finance, and sales, and work backward from the business outcome rather than forward from the tactic.
  • Curiosity and courage. This one's more a personality trait than a skill, but it's the one I screen for the hardest. We look for marketers who are willing to test, fail, and ditch playbooks that worked before — and learn.

Together, these might mean being willing to challenge past marketing practices, or refusing to delegate the strategic judgment that only your team can provide.

Own your data. Don't outsource your judgment

This evolution in capability directly reshapes how a modern marketing organization must handle its operational intelligence. As AI increases the sheer volume of information available, it's more critical than ever to have internal teams with the business context to ask the right questions.

Here's a belief I hold that might ruffle some feathers: you cannot outsource the interpretation of your own data.

There is real value in outside expertise, but no third party can understand your business, customers, and strategy as well as your team does. Even the best external partners optimize for what they can see. They can't fully comprehend what your business actually values, which customers you're trying to reach, or which tradeoffs make sense for your strategy. That knowledge lives inside your team.

That's why we made the call to bring our marketing analytics and data science capabilities in-house.

External agencies gave us a strong starting point, but taking full control of our marketing mix models allowed us to apply our own deeper business context. As our company evolved, we identified legacy channels that were no longer driving meaningful customer growth. Left unchecked, those kinds of disconnects can lead to expensive decisions.

Data should inform decisions. It should not replace human judgment, taste, or creative risk-taking. This distinction will only become more important.

The advantage will not come from having more dashboards or more data points. It will come from having people who can separate signal from noise and know what questions to ask next.

A challenge for marketing leaders

For my fellow marketing leaders, this evolution demands a different kind of leadership.

Consumer behavior has changed. Media has changed. AI is changing how people discover information and make decisions.

We must build the courage to break our own systems and challenge our own assumptions. The playbooks that served us a few years ago won't necessarily produce the right outcomes today. We must treat marketing less as a collection of best practices and more as a science, while fostering a culture that encourages creative experimentation.

That's what I believe the hiring data is really telling us. Companies aren't hiring fewer marketers because marketing matters less. They're hiring differently because the role itself is changing. The future won't belong to marketers who simply know how to run yesterday's playbook. It will belong to those with the judgment to evolve, take risks, and be bold.

Covering a sprawling festival like TIFF solo is next to impossible, so I do my best to see as much as I can, and then write about everything with bite-sized reviews published each day. For 2026, that means exciting upcoming films like Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother , The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , and a gigantic Elon Musk documentary, and even a few streaming series, like Crystal Lake and Carrie . You can keep up with my thoughts on everything I watch right here. items.title: New York Seizes 12 Celebrity Deepfake Websites
items.summary: The New York District Attorney announced on Monday that it has seized 12 websites hosting AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery, primarily of celebrities and public figures. The DA’s office said it believes that this marks the largest seizure of such sites in history. The people using and running these sites who are now under investigation used AI tools to turn approximately 1,200 people’s photos into “hyper-realistic” images and videos of them engaged in sexual conduct, according to the DA’s office. The images allegedly depicted “politicians, first ladies of multiple countries, primarily public-facing individuals, including actors, politicians, athletes, musicians, social justice advocates, and social media influencers. New York has had laws specifically criminalizing sexually explicit deepfakes in place since 2023. Bragg referenced this legislation when asked what law the office is acting on. “While the victims of these sites are largely celebrities, we know that anyone can be a victim in these crimes, particularly in domestic violence cases, many of our intimate violence cases involve threats to at least images and videos, and we know that deepfakes are being used in the same way,” District Attorney Alvin Bragg said in the press conference Monday. “So, whoever you are, the message to survivors is the same: You are not alone. Help is available. If you let us know that an image has been posted without your permission, without your consent, we can take action as long as that website is accessible from Manhattan.” Bragg declined to answer whether images of minors were included in these websites, saying, “The investigation is ongoing.” In June , the U.S. Departments of Justice and Homeland Security seized two domains that were being used to publish “thousands of digitally forged images and videos depicting famous women as nude and sometimes engaged in sexual activity, without their consent,” and featured topics like “rape,” “forced,” and “degradation,” according to a press release. Images on those sites allegedly depicted politicians, first ladies of multiple countries, royalty, journalists, television presenters, athletes, entertainers, and others. And in May 2025, the massive deepfakes hosting site and forum MrDeepfakes.com shut down following an investigation by the Canadian Broadcasting Company, Der Spiegel, and Bellingcat. Earlier this month, the first man in the country to be convicted of violating the Take It Down Act was sentenced to 15 years in prison, after investigators found more than 3,000 real and AI-generated abuse images on his devices. Slightly altered images of women who are public figures are taking over social media sites like X.com, 404 Media reported last month . These images are often not completely nude AI images of women, or face-swapped sexual material, but depict women as wearing more revealing clothing than they did in the real photo or video, or with digitally altered bodies. The DA’s office is encouraging victims of deepfakes to contact its Cyber Crime Bureau at (212) 335-9600. Bragg said targets of deepfakes might not know that something can be done, and wants them to know there’s a “cop on the beat.” “Our message to the people who are creating and publishing this content: What you are doing is a crime. We are investigating, and support survivors in taking down this content and seeking accountability for folks who break the law,” Bragg said.

items.title: 'Diary of a CEO' star Steven Bartlett will bet up to $400 million to build a new generation of star creators
items.summary: Steven Bartlett, host of "Diary of a CEO," wants to apply his playbook to other creators. Sam Barnes/Sportsfile for Web Summit Qatar via Getty Images Podcaster Steven Bartlett is joining with Authentic Brands to help creators grow their businesses. They announced a venture called OBSN that will invest up to $400 million in creators. Bartlett has tried to apply his success to other creators before, with podcast network FlightStory. Podcast star Steven Bartlett is joining with Authentic Brands Group to invest up to $400 million to help other creators grow their businesses. The host of "The Diary of A CEO" podcast — through his holding company, Steven.com — on Monday unveiled OBSN. The venture will provide creators with capital, infrastructure, and expertise. OBSN also includes a creator-economy media platform, which Bartlett's company will run. It features news, analysis, and live experiences. Authentic, meanwhile, will handle the brand-building, product, licensing, strategic partnerships, and global distribution sides of the operation. The pitch is that the new venture will combine Bartlett's experience building creator-led media with Authentic's history of managing brands and intellectual property. Authentic invests in IP and cultural assets. Its portfolio includes more than 50 brands and figures, including Reebok, Shaquille O'Neal, Sports Illustrated, and Elvis Presley. Bartlett said the venture was an attempt to answer what he called a problem of "fragmentation vultures," partners who help creators with different aspects of their businesses but who have misaligned interests. "Is it possible to have a truly integrated partner?" he said onstage, announcing the initiative. "We believe there is." Bartlett said offstage that he'd look for creators who operate in evergreen categories and score highly on traits like resilience, ambition, and the ability to respond to setbacks. "I almost see creators as founders now, because they're operating in these multi-hyphenated businesses," he said. Jamie Salter, executive chairman of Authentic, said his company's value to creators lies in playing more than just an agent role. "Can we take this creator economy and do what we've done with David Beckham or Marilyn Monroe or Shaquille O'Neal and take your brand across all these different pillars?" Salter said. "We are a one-stop shop." The number of creators the money will be spread across hasn't yet been determined, and the companies didn't commit to a detailed timeframe beyond saying funds would be deployed "over the coming years." Bartlett is best known for his 9-year-old podcast "The Diary of a CEO," which has amassed about 20 million subscribers on YouTube, approaching Joe Rogan, and has become the No. 1 business podcast on Spotify in the US. It's not the first time Bartlett has tried to leverage his own social media success to build other creators' businesses. With one of his companies, FlightStory, he's been signing and nurturing other talent. He's sought to apply his own playbook to their businesses, including extensive pre-show research and using social clipping to grow their footprints. His first big test case is "Hot Smart Rich" host Maggie Sellers Reum, whom he recently invested seven figures in through FlightStory. His company has a speakers division, called FlightSpeakers , and a unit that helps other creators distribute on social media. FlightStory is also exploring a paid membership program to tap into diehard fans. Bartlett recently raised an eight-figure investment round to expand the company, which has about 150 employees and took in around $47 million in revenue last year. items.title: A 27-year-old AI researcher shot to fame after speaking out against AI's threat to humanity. Was it a smart career move?
items.summary: A stock image of a software engineer at work; it does not depict Jacob Coxon. Deagreez/Getty Images Quitting Anthropic may have made Jacob Coxon one of AI's hottest free agents. A viral warning can turn a little-known researcher into a public name. His options: joining another lab, building a career in AI safety, or founding something of his own. Didn’t know who Jacob Coxon was a couple of weeks ago? You're not alone. As of last week, the 27-year-old former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher has become the poster child for AI panic. In an X post on Tuesday, Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic, saying that neither AI lab was "acting responsibly" and both were "gambling with our lives." In an interview with The Daily published on Monday, Coxon said he initially wanted to resign without making a statement. "I'd never posted online before, on Twitter, on public social media," Coxon said. "So this was kind of my first ever post. But I was like, I guess I should say something." The post went viral, drawing more than 171 million views on X and catapulting Coxon from relative obscurity into the role of AI's latest doomsayer. It also has the makings of a smart career move. 'He'll have no shortage of offers' Lawrence Rosenberg, a London-based communications specialist who focuses on AI leaders, said Coxon’s sudden prominence could make him a highly sought-after hire. “He’s likely given up a six-figure job, but he’ll have no shortage of offers because he now offers something more than just an AI researcher,” Rosenberg told Business Insider. “Jacob Coxon has a personal brand built around moral conscientiousness.” Rosenberg said Coxon has quickly established himself as a relatable messenger with a ground-level perspective . He's seen as "a real human who's curbing his personal ambition for the good of you and me," Rosenberg said. That "good guy" persona, he said, could make Coxon catnip for companies keen to signal a serious commitment to AI safety. “Wherever he goes next, his employment screams to the world, ‘these are the good guys,’” Rosenberg added. “That company will get organic coverage that would’ve cost millions in advertising.” It could give some employers pause, or he could go at it alone Matthew McGrigor, a recruiter at New York-based tech search firm Worth Search, said Coxon's public callout of OpenAI and Anthropic could give some employers pause. "I doubt he would care about that right now," he said, given how forcefully Coxon has argued against private companies driving the race to superintelligence. For some researchers leaving frontier labs, the next step is not a move to another commercial AI company, but a career at a mission-led nonprofit. On Thursday, two researchers from Anthropic and Google DeepMind left their safety teams to join METR , a nonprofit research group founded by a former OpenAI researcher. While Coxon worked in pretraining rather than AI safety, his public stance could still make him an attractive recruit for the growing safety ecosystem. McGrigor predicted that a safety-focused lab would "snap him up within the next few weeks." In his interview with The Daily, Coxon said he'd had discussions with Anthropic's safety teams and considered working with them before he quit. Coxon could also ultimately choose to go at it alone, building his own safety-focused venture, Kelly Gauthier, managing director at the London-based AI executive-search firm Higher, told Business Insider. For a new company to be viable, Gauthier said, venture capitalists would need to see a clear investment opportunity. "Safety and governance and growth don't necessarily go hand in hand, so that will be an important contradiction to resolve," she said. A smart career move? As the debate around the AI apocalypse accelerates, Coxon is not alone in facing a quit-or-stay conundrum. The decision is more complicated than it may seem, as Sarah E. Needleman wrote for Business Insider . Coxon, who didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider, is not the first tech insider to discover that a public break with a powerful company can be a career accelerator. Sarah Wynn-Williams turned her time inside Facebook into "Careless People," a bestselling memoir that made her one of Big Tech's most prominent public critics. After Leopold Aschenbrenner was fired by OpenAI in 2024 over an alleged information leak, which he disputes, he went on to publish a viral memo titled "Situational Awareness." It subsequently became the name of his AI-focused hedge fund, which suffered steep losses over the summer after an initial meteoric rise. And in 2020, when Timnit Gebru was pushed out of Google's Ethical AI team, the discourse around her departure made her a big name in AI ethics. So much so that in 2023, she was named to TIME's list of the world's 100 most influential people. There is, of course, a precedent for turning AI-safety concerns into a lucrative business venture: Anthropic itself. It was founded by former OpenAI researchers who wanted to promote AI safety. The Amodeis are now multibillionaires. Anthropic is targeting an IPO in October . As for Coxon, McGrigor said he's unlikely to be hard-up in his career after Anthropic. "He'll have options," McGrigor said. "It ultimately comes down to finding an organization whose risk tolerance and mission align with his personal stance." items.title: Prehistoric builders transported Devil's Arrows 11 miles
items.summary: Stonehenge is the most famous example of megalithic architecture across Britain and Ireland, but there are plenty of others, including Calanais, Newgrange, and Avebury, as well as the Devil's Arrows. The latter is Britain's tallest standing stone alignment, yet little is known about the provenance of its stones. Scientists have confirmed that the stones came from a site 18 kilometers (11 miles) away, transported by humans rather than glacial movement, according to a paper published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences. "Sites in southern England and Scotland receive considerable attention but monuments like the Devil's Arrows have remained comparatively understudied despite their significance," said co-author Jim Leary of the University of York. "We have now proved that Neolithic communities moved several 25-ton stones across Yorkshire, transforming a familiar site into an epic quest to create a sacred landscape." Stonehenge has been the focus of recent chemical analyses identifying where all the stones that make up the structure came from, revealing that many originated in quarries a significant distance away. For instance, a 2019 study concluded that the 42 bluestones that make up the inner ring came all the way from western Wales. The outer layer of sarsen stones hails from much closer to home: Marlborough Downs, an area of round, grassy hills 25 to 30 km (17 miles) north of Stonehenge, which has the largest concentration of sarsen in the UK. Read full article Comments

items.title: Killer AI: Yours for $50 per million output tokens and a side of CTO ennui
items.summary: The Stack writes for sober people like the CIOs, CTOs, CISOs and SVPs running enterprise technology programmes at large banks, defense organisations, or pharmaceutical companies. We also speak to them regularly at private events. These deeply experienced adults have typically seen more than a few hype cycles come and go. They’ve raised a wry eyebrow as people claim that cartoons of apes are the very future of finance; sometimes learned the hard way that lifting and shifting onto the public cloud is a recipe for nasty bill shock; been told that “data is the new oil” too many times to count (indeed: typically polluted and expensive to refine), and smiled politely as someone sells them another “military-grade encrypted,” “single pane of glass.” Now they’re being told AI will kill them soon without urgent regulatory intervention . But meanwhile, “pssssst, try the enterprise-ready version of the apocalypse machine for just $50 per million output tokens” (and can we have another 100 nuclear power station-equivalents in the UK alone, to power this nascent death star please? It might also cure cancer...) The real AI fear Most members of our community are largely eschewing the cognitive dissonance raised by this jarring death-and-tokens messaging, and focusing on the near-term AI challenges of their day jobs. The Stack will try to do the same, despite the mounting Silicon Valley hysteria. After all, those challenges are manifold...

items.title: Build anywhere, stay in flow: How Windows 365 is redefining the developer experience
items.summary: Development teams are under increasing pressure to ship software faster, even as the environments they rely on grow more complex. However, modern development has only become harder to provision and maintain with AI-assisted development, cross-platform toolchains, tighter security demands and specialized compute requirements. As a result, developers still spend too much time configuring machines, troubleshooting environment drift, and waiting for access instead of building and shipping software. Windows 365 provides secure, flexible Cloud PCs that can complement local development and give teams an easier path from access to first commit. Developers can select an environment suited to each workload while IT applies consistent identity, security, management and governance. Five ways Windows 365 supports modern development 1. Give developers a ready-to-code, customizable environment A ready-to-code Windows 11 developer configuration provides developers with a prepared environment from day one. Autopilot device preparation can install required applications and scripts before first sign-in, while Azure Compute Gallery integration supports standardized custom images. Planned VM customization will provide additional flexibility to configure project-specific SDKs, tools, scripts, and dependencies within enterprise guardrails. 2. Scale compute and run local AI directly on the Cloud PC Cloud PC configurations up to 32 vCPU and GPU-enabled options give teams the right compute for memory-intensive development, graphics, AI, data and visualization workloads. Select local language models can run directly on appropriately sized Cloud PCs, providing more predictable costs while preserving access to hosted models when greater scale or performance is required. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M-WDKwkGuZc See how a ready-to-code Windows 365 Cloud PC uses Foundry Local and local language models to build and run an AI meeting-summary app without consuming cloud tokens. 3. Contain agent activity during development Developers increasingly use coding and autonomous agents to generate code, execute tasks and maintain long-running workflows. With Windows 365 support for Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) becoming generally available in the coming months, customers will be able to run supported agent workloads, from coding agents such as GitHub Copilot CLI to autonomous agents such as OpenClaw on managed Cloud PCs. Process and session isolation help contain agent activity, while familiar enterprise security and governance controls allow organizations to manage these workloads with confidence. 4. Build and run enterprise agents securely AI agent builders have different needs. As agents move from development into sustained enterprise workflows, they may require dedicated environments that operate independently from users’ devices. Windows 365 for Agents provides Microsoft Entra-joined, Microsoft Intune-managed, and policy-enforced Cloud PCs where agents can perform computer-use tasks across browsers, desktop applications, and legacy systems. New preview capabilities extend secure access to on-premises applications and help IT manage agent pools at scale . Companies such as Login VSI , WorkspaceDNA , and Simular are already building AI agents that can run on Windows 365 for Agents. 5. Protect sensitive development work Organizations need to give developers flexibility without exposing source code or confidential data. Windows 365 works with Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Intune, and Microsoft security capabilities to apply consistent identity, access, compliance and endpoint controls. For example, context-based redirection , now in preview can restrict clipboard, drive, printer or USB redirection based on security conditions, while output protection helps safeguard on-screen information. Why m odern development needs an environment that resp ond s to c ha nge As development workflows evolve in the era of AI, d evelopers need different environments based on workloads. Local devices remain essential for developers when direct hardware access, offline work, or specialized local performance matters. Pairing the latest in hardware innovation with software optimized for development helps developers build breakthrough experiences. Project Zenith offers a ready-to-code distraction-free Windows experience on developer-class devices with 64+ GB unified memory and 250+ GB/s memory bandwidth, so developers can get started. And c loud -based environments can complement local development when continuity across devices, workload isolation, flexible compute , or secure access creates a better outcome. Developers should be able to choose the environment best suited to their work while maintaining a consistent, trusted development experience. A developer may move between coding, compute-intensive builds and testing, AI-augmented application development, and work in a secure customer environment . Each workload benefit s from an environment optimized for its specific requirement s . Windows 365 brings the right environment to developers A modern developer environment should allow developers to begin coding on day one, support customization for specific projects and provide secure governance without limiting developer flexibility. Windows 365 brings these capabilities together in a personalized Cloud PC that developers can access through the Windows App or a browser, while their applications, code, settings and project state remain securely managed in the Microsoft Cloud. With Windows 365, developers can start with a Windows 11 developer configuration featuring familiar tools such as Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub Copilot CLI, Python, Node.js and Windows Subsystem for Linux with Ubuntu. Meanwhile, platform engineering and IT teams can standardize environments with reusable images and automated preparation while centrally managing identity, security, policy, monitoring, and lifecycle controls. The result is more than a desktop in the cloud: it is a faster path from access to first commit. Customers are already seeing this balance of developer flexibility and enterprise control in practice: London Stock Exchange Group increases developer productivity with Windows 365 . “Windows 365 gives us the ability to provide different types of performance and development environments plus access to GitHub Copilot, where we’ve seen an increase in developer productivity and efficiency.” says Sandra Lee, Group Chief Information Security Officer, LSEG. Siemens uses Windows 365 for scenarios that include developers who need specialized digital tools, as well as employees requiring temporary access . “In all these cases, we need a trustworthy device and a verified identity in our IT landscape—even if the access is only intended to be temporary,” says Hendrik Harder, Global Service Owner Virtual Client at Siemens. ABN AMRO transforms the workplace for 3,500 offshore developers with Windows 365. Developers reported smoother performance, faster onboarding and more productivity, while IT teams benefited from simplified operations and scalability. “The first time I used Windows 365, I thought I was using my own laptop—the performance was that smooth,” says Peter Witmond, Product Owner Virtual Workplace at ABN AMRO. Advancing developer experiences with Windows 365 on a unified platform Microsoft is bringing cloud development environments together on a single platform. With the retirement of Microsoft Dev Box, Windows 365 becomes Microsoft's strategic platform for virtualized developer environments, AI and agent workloads, and the broader workforce. While existing Dev Box customers can continue using their deployments according to the official service timeline , Windows 365 offers a broader, unified foundation for developers and organizations moving forward. Dev Box proved what developers need: environments that combine developer flexibility with enterprise control. Windows 365 carries these promises forward and extends them across developers, information workers, AI builders and agents through a shared foundation for identity, security, management, and access models. That shared foundation is what makes the next generation of developer Cloud PCs possible. ​‌ Turning workload choice into a modern developer workflow With Windows 365, organizations can start with a ready-to-code environment, match compute to each workload, contain agent activity during development, provide dedicated environments for enterprise agents and apply consistent controls to protect sensitive work. Start with a scenario where setup delays, hardware constraints or security requirements slow delivery, and measure improvements in onboarding, time to first commit, support requests, or build performance. Explore Windows 365 developer resources and review the official Microsoft Dev Box guidance .

items.title: More choice and possibility with Windows PCs at IFA
items.summary:
This year at IFA, I saw the Windows ecosystem doing what it does best: bringing innovation to life through products and experiences for every person, purpose, and price point. Our partners introduced new Windows PCs, spanning dependable everyday devices, beautifully crafted premium designs, new and immersive gaming systems, commercial devices designed to help organizations work securely and productively, and powerful tools for developers, creators, and AI power users. Together, these announcements demonstrated the breadth of what’s possible with a Windows PC. This matters because people are being thoughtful about when, where, and how they spend. We know that a new PC is a meaningful purchase, and that customers want to feel confident that they choose the right PC for them. They want to know that it will deliver a better experience today while continuing to meet their needs for years to come. Windows PCs from our partners give people more ways to find the right device without compromising on what matters most to them. Innovation available today For more than 40 years, our goal has been to put a computer on every desk and in every home. We know the PC is personal and the place you go to play, create, build, connect and learn. Some prioritize battery life and portability, while others need greater performance for gaming or creative work. And increasingly, people are also looking for useful AI experiences that are easy to use and fit seamlessly into their existing workflows. And of course, everyone needs to find the right device at the right price for them. IFA showed how our partners are meeting those different needs. The strength of Windows is choice, and the latest Windows PCs bring together modern design, stronger performance, built-in security and useful AI experiences available at different price points. items.title: Steam Frame: The Ars Technica review
items.summary: In the 2010s, Valve was at the forefront of a virtual reality revolution that looked to some like it would upend the gaming industry. The Valve of six to ten years ago seemed committed to being a major player in the world of PC-connected VR headsets, first through its “strategic partnership” with HTC on the impressive-for-the-time Vive headset (plus the SteamVR platform standard that powered it) and then years later with its own Index headset (and proof-of-concept adventure Half-Life: Alyx ). Then came the Meta (previously Oculus) Quest , a low-powered, low-cost headset that proved the vast majority of VR-curious gamers didn’t want to bother with being literally tethered to a bulky, expensive gaming PC. As the Quest line carved out a modest niche through the 2020s, Valve seemed more or less satisfied to let its earlier VR hardware and software ambitions wither on the vine. Those years of Valve’s benign neglect of VR make the imminent release of the $1,049 Steam Frame—which starts taking reservations today—more than a little surprising. Now that virtual reality’s hype-fueled, revolutionary promises have decidedly not played out , Valve is somehow ready and willing to limp headfirst into the world of standalone VR headsets—today, in 2026. And after spending a week or so with Valve’s latest foray into gaming hardware, the Frame somehow feels simultaneously overengineered and underbaked, depending on how you look at it. Read full article Comments

items.title: Trump's swing at green card holders on public benefits is facing a slew of lawsuits
items.summary: The Trump administration is pushing to deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits. Alex Wong/Getty Images States and cities are suing the Trump administration over a policy to restrict green card access. The policy could mean immigrants could be denied green cards for nearly any use of public benefits. New York City, Chicago, San Francisco, and Seattle hope to block the policy from going into effect. A coalition of states and local governments is suing the Trump administration over plans to limit green cards for immigrants enrolled in public benefits. The two lawsuits, filed Monday, say the White House is upending decades of legal precedent governing social safety nets and sparking fear and confusion. Set to go into effect on September 18, Trump's policy would allow federal officers to consider whether an applicant has used — or is likely to use — public benefits during their green card application process. The suits seek to block the Department of Homeland Security and federal leaders from considering an individual's use of benefits in these applications. New York City, Chicago, San Francisco, and Seattle are among the plaintiffs, as are several states. Typically, eligibility for federal aid programs — such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program , housing vouchers, and Medicaid — is based on household income and size. Many immigrants do not qualify for social safety net programs, and the programs are fully unavailable to undocumented people. Even after they have a green card, it can take years for immigrants to be legally allowed to claim benefits. Still, plaintiffs say a policy like this could discourage immigrant families with US-born children from enrolling for food or healthcare assistance. It's not the first time the administration has taken steps to limit avenues for immigration. The White House hoped to institute a $100,000 H-1B visa fee for employers, which was most recently blocked by an appeals court. Companies like Meta, Google, and Amazon have slashed H-1B petitions after Trump's visa crackdown. Economists have also pointed toward declining immigration as a reason for declining labor force participation this year. Read the original article on Business Insider

  • States and cities are suing the Trump administration over a policy to restrict green card access.
  • The policy could mean immigrants could be denied green cards for nearly any use of public benefits.
  • New York City, Chicago, San Francisco, and Seattle hope to block the policy from going into effect.

A coalition of states and local governments is suing the Trump administration over plans to limit green cards for immigrants enrolled in public benefits.

The two lawsuits, filed Monday, say the White House is upending decades of legal precedent governing social safety nets and sparking fear and confusion. Set to go into effect on September 18, Trump's policy would allow federal officers to consider whether an applicant has used — or is likely to use — public benefits during their green card application process.

The suits seek to block the Department of Homeland Security and federal leaders from considering an individual's use of benefits in these applications.

New York City, Chicago, San Francisco, and Seattle are among the plaintiffs, as are several states.

Typically, eligibility for federal aid programs — such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, housing vouchers, and Medicaid — is based on household income and size.

Many immigrants do not qualify for social safety net programs, and the programs are fully unavailable to undocumented people. Even after they have a green card, it can take years for immigrants to be legally allowed to claim benefits. Still, plaintiffs say a policy like this could discourage immigrant families with US-born children from enrolling for food or healthcare assistance.

It's not the first time the administration has taken steps to limit avenues for immigration. The White House hoped to institute a $100,000 H-1B visa fee for employers, which was most recently blocked by an appeals court. Companies like Meta, Google, and Amazon have slashed H-1B petitions after Trump's visa crackdown.

Economists have also pointed toward declining immigration as a reason for declining labor force participation this year.

items.title: AI has arrived in South Africa’s boardrooms – but company law hasn’t caught up
items.summary: Werner Pfennig/Pexels AI is beginning to influence how boards of directors make decisions in South African companies . Directors use it to do things like assess financial information, predict market trends or identify potential risks before making strategic decisions. But there is a problem. South African company law does not regulate its use by boards. This matters in relation to the rules governing directors’ duties and responsibilities. Many countries already regulate AI through binding legislation. For example, the European Union , South Korea and Vietnam adopted comprehensive AI laws. Other countries such as China introduced more  targeted AI regulations. As a company law researcher, in a recent paper I looked at four company law implications of AI use in South African boardrooms: whether by consulting AI the board will be regarded as having complied with its fiduciary duties whether directors can rely on the business judgment rule in section 76(4) of the Companies Act when AI-assisted decisions result in negative consequences for the company whether directors can lawfully delegate their functions to AI, and rely on AI-generated advice without incurring liability for incorrect decisions made by those systems who is liable when AI errors cause harm to third parties. In other words, who is legally responsible for the consequences of decisions that AI makes? My findings show that current South African law provides little guidance on these issues. As AI becomes part of everyday business, this gap is becoming a legal and governance challenge. Clear legal rules are urgently needed to prevent a legal vacuum being created in South African boardrooms. How AI can assist boards There are different ways in which boards can use AI to manage companies and make decisions. The simplest form is assisted AI . It performs administrative tasks while directors retain control over decision-making. It can compile meeting agendas, call meetings and draft reports. This allows directors to focus on strategic decisions. Augmented AI can analyse large amounts of information, identify trends and predict the likely outcomes of different business decisions. For example, it could analyse data and evaluate the risks of a merger and recommend the best course of action. The AI provides recommendations, but the board still makes the final decision. The most advanced form is autonomous AI , which can make decisions and carry out tasks without constant human input. Boards could, for example, authorise an AI system to make investment decisions within set parameters and independently monitor markets and execute trades. AI has important limits Although AI has advantages in supporting corporate decision-making, my research found that it has limitations too. These may affect the reliability of AI-generated recommendations. AI systems learn from existing data. If that data is inaccurate or biased, AI’s recommendations could also be biased. This is a concern in South Africa, where historical inequalities remain reflected in many datasets . A 2024 study by the Centre of Excellence in Financial Services suggested that AI used in South African banking could perpetuate racial bias. If companies rely on it without proper oversight, AI could repeat or worsen existing discrimination patterns. Another challenge is that many AI systems operate as a “ black box ”. They may produce sophisticated recommendations, but even their developers may struggle to explain how the AI systems reached a particular conclusion. A further limitation is that AI lacks human qualities essential for effective board leadership , such as empathy, intuition and emotional intelligence. Can directors delegate their functions to AI? South African company law allows directors to delegate certain functions to others. But they cannot relinquish their ultimate responsibility for managing the company. They remain accountable for board decisions. My research argues that the same principle should apply to AI. Directors should be allowed to delegate their functions to assisted AI and perhaps augmented AI, provided they properly supervise the AI system and do not relinquish their responsibilities. But delegation to autonomous AI should not be allowed. If directors delegated their functions to it, they would be giving AI decision-making powers and giving up their responsibilities. Directors cannot simply accept AI recommendations. Company law requires them to exercise independent judgment . They must also act in the company’s best interests . If they can’t  understand how AI reached a recommendation, how will they determine whether it is in the company’s best interests? In my view, directors should therefore have some AI literacy. They do not need to understand the coding in detail. But they should have enough AI literacy to understand how the AI works. This will enable them to properly supervise the delegation of their functions to AI. Who is liable when AI gets it wrong? An important legal question is determining responsibility when AI causes harm. Imagine management uses AI to assist in recommending an investment to the board. The board approves the investment based on that AI-generated recommendation, but the investment results in substantial losses. Who should be held liable? The AI system itself cannot be sued because it is not a legal person . It cannot own property, pay damages or appear before a court . Responsibility could potentially fall on the company, the software developer or directors who relied on the AI system. Directors might be held liable if they failed to supervise the AI system properly, but the Companies Act does not clearly define where responsibility begins or ends. This uncertainty creates risks. Companies need legal certainty before investing in AI. Directors need clear guidance about their duties, while those affected by AI-driven decisions need to know who is accountable if something goes wrong. Without clear legal rules, disputes are likely to increase as AI becomes more common in corporate decision-making. South Africa should act now South Africa has taken some steps. The National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework promotes ethical, transparent and human-centred AI. The Draft National AI Policy is pending. It was published for public comment in April 2026 but was withdrawn after fictitious AI-generated sources were discovered in the reference list. The King V Code on Corporate Governance for South Africa 2025 also recommends that boards should ensure that AI is used ethically, transparently, fairly, securely and with clear human oversight. In my view, these developments are important, but they are not enough. The Companies Act should be updated to reflect AI’s growing role in corporate decision-making. The Companies Act should require directors to supervise decisions made by AI. Ultimate human control of the AI system should be legally required. My research argues that provision should be made for directors to rely on assisted and augmented AI, but not autonomous AI, subject to the directors supervising the AI and exercising an independent judgment. The Companies Act should  require directors to have a sufficient level of AI literacy. Boards should appoint at least one member with AI expertise. Companies should be required to appoint a designated AI officer responsible for the safe, ethical and unbiased use of AI. Companies should also consider taking out insurance against potential liabilities arising from AI-generated decisions. Rehana Cassim does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

But there is a problem. South African company law does not regulate its use by boards. This matters in relation to the rules governing directors’ duties and responsibilities.

Many countries already regulate AI through binding legislation. For example, the European Union, South Korea and Vietnam adopted comprehensive AI laws. Other countries such as China introduced more targeted AI regulations.

As a company law researcher, in a recent paper I looked at four company law implications of AI use in South African boardrooms:

  • whether by consulting AI the board will be regarded as having complied with its fiduciary duties

  • whether directors can rely on the business judgment rule in section 76(4) of the Companies Act when AI-assisted decisions result in negative consequences for the company

  • whether directors can lawfully delegate their functions to AI, and rely on AI-generated advice without incurring liability for incorrect decisions made by those systems

  • who is liable when AI errors cause harm to third parties. In other words, who is legally responsible for the consequences of decisions that AI makes?

My findings show that current South African law provides little guidance on these issues. As AI becomes part of everyday business, this gap is becoming a legal and governance challenge. Clear legal rules are urgently needed to prevent a legal vacuum being created in South African boardrooms.

How AI can assist boards

There are different ways in which boards can use AI to manage companies and make decisions.

The simplest form is assisted AI. It performs administrative tasks while directors retain control over decision-making. It can compile meeting agendas, call meetings and draft reports. This allows directors to focus on strategic decisions.

Augmented AI can analyse large amounts of information, identify trends and predict the likely outcomes of different business decisions. For example, it could analyse data and evaluate the risks of a merger and recommend the best course of action. The AI provides recommendations, but the board still makes the final decision.

The most advanced form is autonomous AI, which can make decisions and carry out tasks without constant human input. Boards could, for example, authorise an AI system to make investment decisions within set parameters and independently monitor markets and execute trades.

AI has important limits

Although AI has advantages in supporting corporate decision-making, my research found that it has limitations too. These may affect the reliability of AI-generated recommendations.

AI systems learn from existing data. If that data is inaccurate or biased, AI’s recommendations could also be biased. This is a concern in South Africa, where historical inequalities remain reflected in many datasets.

A 2024 study by the Centre of Excellence in Financial Services suggested that AI used in South African banking could perpetuate racial bias. If companies rely on it without proper oversight, AI could repeat or worsen existing discrimination patterns.

Another challenge is that many AI systems operate as a “black box”. They may produce sophisticated recommendations, but even their developers may struggle to explain how the AI systems reached a particular conclusion.

A further limitation is that AI lacks human qualities essential for effective board leadership, such as empathy, intuition and emotional intelligence.

Can directors delegate their functions to AI?

South African company law allows directors to delegate certain functions to others. But they cannot relinquish their ultimate responsibility for managing the company. They remain accountable for board decisions.

My research argues that the same principle should apply to AI. Directors should be allowed to delegate their functions to assisted AI and perhaps augmented AI, provided they properly supervise the AI system and do not relinquish their responsibilities.

But delegation to autonomous AI should not be allowed. If directors delegated their functions to it, they would be giving AI decision-making powers and giving up their responsibilities.

Directors cannot simply accept AI recommendations. Company law requires them to exercise independent judgment. They must also act in the company’s best interests. If they can’t understand how AI reached a recommendation, how will they determine whether it is in the company’s best interests?

In my view, directors should therefore have some AI literacy. They do not need to understand the coding in detail. But they should have enough AI literacy to understand how the AI works. This will enable them to properly supervise the delegation of their functions to AI.

An important legal question is determining responsibility when AI causes harm.

Imagine management uses AI to assist in recommending an investment to the board. The board approves the investment based on that AI-generated recommendation, but the investment results in substantial losses. Who should be held liable?

The AI system itself cannot be sued because it is not a legal person. It cannot own property, pay damages or appear before a court.

Responsibility could potentially fall on the company, the software developer or directors who relied on the AI system. Directors might be held liable if they failed to supervise the AI system properly, but the Companies Act does not clearly define where responsibility begins or ends.

This uncertainty creates risks. Companies need legal certainty before investing in AI. Directors need clear guidance about their duties, while those affected by AI-driven decisions need to know who is accountable if something goes wrong.

Without clear legal rules, disputes are likely to increase as AI becomes more common in corporate decision-making.

South Africa should act now

South Africa has taken some steps. The National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework promotes ethical, transparent and human-centred AI. The Draft National AI Policy is pending. It was published for public comment in April 2026 but was withdrawn after fictitious AI-generated sources were discovered in the reference list.

The King V Code on Corporate Governance for South Africa 2025 also recommends that boards should ensure that AI is used ethically, transparently, fairly, securely and with clear human oversight.

In my view, these developments are important, but they are not enough. The Companies Act should be updated to reflect AI’s growing role in corporate decision-making.

The Companies Act should require directors to supervise decisions made by AI. Ultimate human control of the AI system should be legally required.

My research argues that provision should be made for directors to rely on assisted and augmented AI, but not autonomous AI, subject to the directors supervising the AI and exercising an independent judgment.

The Companies Act should require directors to have a sufficient level of AI literacy. Boards should appoint at least one member with AI expertise. Companies should be required to appoint a designated AI officer responsible for the safe, ethical and unbiased use of AI.

Companies should also consider taking out insurance against potential liabilities arising from AI-generated decisions.

items.title: The best outfits and status symbols celebrities wore at the 2026 US Open
items.summary: Jordyn Woods at the 2026 US Open. Stephanie Augello/Getty Images Fashion was served at the US Open in Queens, New York. Celebrities like Kaia Gerber aced their looks by wearing flashy pieces, such as Cartier watches. And it didn't matter that spring is over — florals were in. It was game on at the US Open this year. The annual tennis tournament kicked off in Queens, New York, on August 23 and ended on September 13. While some had their eyes glued to athletes on the court throughout, the rest of us focused on celebrities in the stands . Businesswoman Martha Stewart, actor Orlando Bloom, and Vogue icon Anna Wintour were all spotted wearing eye-catching outfits and flashy status symbols . Here's a look at their style moments and what other attendees wore. Anna Wintour arrived at the US Open in a Prada trench coat. Anna Wintour at the 2026 US Open. Theo Wargo/Getty Images The tan piece, which featured a red-and-yellow floral print from top to bottom, was made by the Italian fashion brand in 2021. It recently sold on The RealReal for $2,745. She wore it with a tan dress, brown leather boots, and her signature oversize sunglasses. Kaia Gerber sat in the stands and flashed her Cartier watch. Homer Gere and Kaia Gerber at the 2026 US Open. XNY/Star Max/Getty Images The model — and daughter of Cindy Crawford — attended the US Open with actor Homer Gere. She wore a black sleeveless dress, smoky makeup, and a mini Cartier Panthère watch in 18-karat gold, which retails for $28,100. Gayle King paired a floral dress with a metallic Balenciaga bag. Gayle King at the 2026 US Open. Shea Kastriner/Getty Images The TV journalist posed on the event's blue carpet wearing a white sleeveless Yigal Azrouël dress with black stripes and a yellow-and-purple floral print. She also wore yellow pumps, silver jewelry, and carried the $1,400 small Bistro Bag in silver from Balenciaga. Savannah Guthrie was bejeweled with statement accessories. Michael Feldman and Savannah Guthrie at the 2026 US Open. XNY/Star Max/Getty Images The "Today Show" co-host sat in the audience with her husband, Michael Feldman. To complement her black floral dress, Guthrie wore a selection of gold jewelry, including diamond rings, sparkling bracelets, a tennis necklace, and the $11,810 Spiked Heart Sardinia II necklace from Marlo Laz. Serena Williams mixed high and low pieces. Serena Williams at the 2026 US Open. XNY/Star Max/Getty Images While sitting next to Wintour, Williams was photographed wearing the $75 Nike repel windbreaker . Her jewelry, though, was higher-value. She paired diamond earrings and delicate gold necklaces with a Van Cleef Alhambra. Emma Roberts wore top-to-bottom Ferragamo. Emma Roberts at the 2026 US Open. XNY/Star Max/Getty Images The actor walked the US Open carpet in a multi-print sundress from the Italian designer's resort 2027 ready-to-wear line. She also accessorized with the $3,700 Cara bag, the brand's $1,250 bicolor pumps, and dark sunglasses. Orlando Bloom's outfit was the epitome of quiet luxury. Orlando Bloom attends the 2026 US Open. XNY/Star Max/Getty Images From a distance, it looked like Bloom was wearing a simple bomber jacket with jeans and a white T-shirt. His outerwear, though, was actually Prada. He wore the jacket with an $8,250 Porsche Chronograph 1 watch. Bloom is the official ambassador for Porsche Design. Lindsey Vonn had an expensive Rolex timepiece on her wrist. Lindsey Vonn at the 2026 US Open. XNY/Star Max/Getty Images The Olympian ski racer attended the tennis tournament in a green satin gown with a halter neckline and a wrapped skirt. It was the perfect color to complement her blonde hair, and the material shone alongside her Rolex watch. Vonn wore the $160,900 Cosmograph Daytona , which has an Everose gold bracelet and diamonds circling its dial. Travis Scott watched a match while wearing a $2 million watch. Travis Scott at the 2026 US Open. Jean Catuffe/Getty Images The musician sported a rare Richard Mille Flying Tourbillon Sapphire watch, of which only 10 were made. Though the exact model isn't available for sale, similar watches from the brand cost more than $2.5 million. Scott also wore diamond earrings, a Chanel phone holder, and a $135 Cactus Jack x Nike sweatshirt. Common's sunglasses were a highlight of his outfit. Common at the 2026 US Open. Jean Catuffe/Getty Images The musician and actor attended the US Open in a tan, two-piece set with brown stripes. It featured a button-down top with long sleeves and oversize trousers. To match the outfit, he also wore $520 Garland sunglasses from Salt Optics. Alexis Ohanian kept this outfit and accessories simple. Alexis Ohanian at the 2026 US Open. Jean Catuffe/Getty Images The Reddit cofounder (and husband of Serena Williams ) watched his wife's match in a basic outfit that included a black graphic T-shirt, skinny jeans, and Nike sneakers. He also sported a black baseball cap with General Intuition, the name of an AI startup his venture-capital group has invested in, embroidered across it. Martha Stewart perfectly blended activewear with glamour. Martha Stewart at the 2026 US Open. Shea Kastriner/Getty Images Stewart posed for photos while wearing maroon trousers, a green collared shirt, and a plum-colored windbreaker. Her outfit was casual, perfect for a sporting event, and elevated with accessories. She paired it with an assortment of rings, dangling earrings, and a statement gold necklace. Jordyn Woods elevated denim with diamonds. Jordyn Woods at the 2026 US Open. Stephanie Augello/Getty Images The model and entrepreneur posed on the event's red carpet in a denim set from Ralph Lauren and brown accessories. She also flashed a few luxury jewelry pieces, including a thick tennis necklace, an Audemars Piguet watch that costs about $150,000, and her massive engagement ring from her now-husband, Karl-Anthony Towns . Zayn Malik's matching set came from Sandro Paris. Zayn Malik at the 2026 US Open. XNY/Star Max/Getty Images While watching a match on the closing day of the US Open, the former One Direction star wore a $600 denim jacket and $360 jeans from the French brand. Both were brown and featured the Sandro Paris logo all over. Nicole Kidman brought back a skinnier style of jeans. Nicole Kidman at the 2026 US Open. Jean Catuffe/Getty Images The "Practical Magic 2" star wore straight-leg jeans, $1,895 Chanel sneakers, a suede Chanel bag, and a collared shirt from the French fashion house. items.title: What Is Helm? The App Store for Kubernetes (Kubernetes Package Manager)
items.summary: You’ve written Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and Secrets by hand. Helm is what happens when you stop doing that every single time. Familiar, low-intimidation framing that immediately tells a beginner what category of tool this is. Helm packages entire Kubernetes applications — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and more — into reusable, templated charts you can install with one command. Here’s what Helm actually does, how charts work, and when raw YAML is still the better choice. If you’ve worked through the earlier pieces in this series, you’ve now written a Deployment, a Service, a ConfigMap, and a Secret — separately, by hand, as individual YAML files, applied one at a time. That’s a completely reasonable way to learn what each piece actually does. It’s a considerably less reasonable way to deploy a real application, especially once you need to do it more than once, across more than one environment, for more than one person on your team. This is exactly the gap Helm exists to close. And the “app store for Kubernetes” description you’ll see everywhere isn’t just marketing shorthand — it’s a genuinely useful mental model, as long as you understand what’s actually happening underneath that friendly comparison. Helm doesn’t replace the YAML you’ve been learning. It packages it, templates it, and lets you stop retyping it every single time. The Problem Helm Actually Solves Picture deploying something more realistic than a single nginx container — say, an application with a frontend, a backend API, a database, plus the Services, ConfigMaps, and Secrets each of those needs to actually function together. That’s easily ten or more separate YAML files, each one needing to be applied in roughly the right order, each one needing slightly different values depending on whether you’re deploying to development, staging, or production. Now imagine doing that by hand, repeatedly, correctly, every time — and remembering to update the image tag in exactly the right three places when you ship a new version, and remembering which values differ between environments, and not accidentally applying your production ConfigMap values to a staging deployment because you copy-pasted the wrong file. This is where things quietly go wrong in real teams: not because anyone lacks Kubernetes knowledge, but because manually managing dozens of interrelated YAML files at scale is genuinely, tediously error-prone. Key takeaway: Helm isn’t solving a knowledge problem — you already know how to write a Deployment. It’s solving a repetition and consistency problem that shows up the moment “one app” becomes “many YAML files, many times, many environments.” What Helm Actually Is Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes, and that comparison to tools like apt on Linux or Homebrew on macOS is genuinely accurate, not just a friendly analogy. The same way brew install postgresql gets you a working PostgreSQL setup without manually compiling anything yourself, helm install can get you a fully configured, production-ready application running on your cluster — potentially a dozen coordinated Kubernetes resources — with a single command. The package itself is called a chart — a structured bundle of templated YAML files, plus a set of default configuration values, packaged together in a standard, shareable format. Charts exist for an enormous number of common applications already — databases, monitoring stacks, ingress controllers (including the very NGINX Ingress Controller from an earlier article in this series, which most people actually install via Helm rather than raw manifests) — meaning a huge share of “I need to run X on Kubernetes” problems already have a well-maintained chart available before you’d need to write one yourself. Key takeaway: A Helm chart is a packaged, reusable bundle of Kubernetes resources with configurable defaults — the same idea as installing a package with apt or brew, applied to entire applications instead of single binaries. Installing Something With Helm Here’s what using an existing chart actually looks like in practice — installing a real application, in one command, without writing a single line of YAML yourself: # Add a chart repository (a source of charts, similar to adding a package repo) helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami helm repo update # Install a chart — this example deploys a full PostgreSQL setup helm install my-database bitnami/postgresql That single helm install command creates every Kubernetes resource that a properly configured PostgreSQL deployment needs — a StatefulSet, Services, Secrets for credentials, ConfigMaps for configuration, and more — all correctly wired together, without you hand-writing or hand-applying any of it. Check what actually got created: kubectl get all -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=my-database You’ll typically see a genuinely non-trivial number of resources, all created from that one command, all following best practices baked in by whoever maintains that chart — practices you’d otherwise need to research and implement yourself. Key takeaway: helm install on an existing chart turns "research and hand-write a dozen correctly configured YAML files" into "one command," while inheriting configuration best practices from the chart's maintainers. Templates: Where the Real Value Is Installing existing charts is genuinely useful, but the deeper value of Helm shows up once you start writing your own charts for your own applications — and that value comes from templating . Instead of writing a static Deployment YAML with hardcoded values, a Helm chart uses a template with placeholders, filled in from a separate values file at install time: # templates/deployment.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: {{ .Release.Name }}-app spec: replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} selector: matchLabels: app: {{ .Release.Name }} template: metadata: labels: app: {{ .Release.Name }} spec: containers: - name: app image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}" ports: - containerPort: {{ .Values.service.port }} Those double-curly-brace sections are template placeholders, filled in from a values.yaml file: # values.yaml replicaCount: 3 image: repository: my-app tag: "1.4.2" service: port: 8080 This is the actual mechanism behind “reusable deployment package.” The same template produces a correctly configured Deployment whether you’re running 2 replicas in development or 10 in production — you’re not maintaining separate, drifting copies of near-identical YAML files. You maintain one template, and swap in different values files per environment: helm install my-app ./my-chart -f values-production.yaml Key takeaway: The template-plus-values structure is what actually eliminates repetitive YAML — one chart, many environments, driven by different values files instead of duplicated, hand-edited manifests. Upgrades and Rollbacks: The Part People Underestimate Here’s a genuinely underrated Helm capability that doesn’t get mentioned as often as templating: Helm tracks the history of every install and change you make to a given release, which makes upgrading and — critically — rolling back a mistake dramatically simpler than it would be with raw kubectl apply. # Deploy a new version by updating the image tag and re-running helm upgrade my-app ./my-chart --set image.tag=1.5.0 # See the history of every revision helm history my-app # Something's wrong with 1.5.0 — roll back to the previous working revision helm rollback my-app 1 That rollback command is doing real work under the hood — reverting every resource Helm manages for that release back to exactly the configuration it had at the specified revision, not just the image tag. Reproducing that reliably with raw kubectl apply and hand-managed YAML files, especially under the pressure of an active incident, is considerably harder and more error-prone than most people appreciate until they've actually needed it. Key takeaway: Helm’s revision history turns “carefully figure out what changed and manually revert it” into a single rollback command — genuinely valuable during an actual incident, not just a development convenience. Raw YAML:  You write every file --> kubectl apply each one --> hope you remembered them all Helm:      Chart (template + values) --> helm install --> all resources created together, correctly wired, tracked as one release When Raw YAML Is Still the Better Choice It’s worth being honest here, because Helm isn’t strictly better in every situation, and reaching for it prematurely adds real complexity for no real benefit. If you’re still learning what a Deployment, Service, or ConfigMap actually does — which is exactly the stage the earlier articles in this series were built for — writing raw YAML by hand is genuinely the right way to learn it. Templating syntax on top of concepts you haven’t internalized yet just adds a confusing extra layer between you and what’s actually happening. Similarly, for a genuinely simple, single-application deployment that isn’t going to be repeated across multiple environments or maintained by a team, the overhead of chart structure, templating syntax, and values files can outweigh the benefit. Helm earns its complexity budget once you’re dealing with real repetition, real environment differences, or real collaboration — not before. Key takeaway: Helm is a tool for managing complexity and repetition at scale — introducing it before you have either of those problems just trades one kind of overhead for another. Trying It Yourself If you have Helm installed and a cluster running from earlier in this series, the fastest way to see the value directly is creating a starter chart and inspecting what Helm generates for you: helm create my-first-chart This scaffolds a complete, working chart structure — templates, a values.yaml, and sensible defaults — that you can inspect, modify, and install directly: helm install my-release ./my-first-chart kubectl get all -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=my-release Comparing the generated templates against the raw Deployment and Service YAML you wrote by hand earlier in this series is a genuinely useful exercise — you’ll recognize almost everything, just wrapped in template placeholders instead of hardcoded values. The Real Shift Helm Represents The honest way to think about Helm isn’t “a tool that replaces YAML.” It’s a tool that acknowledges a pattern you’ll eventually notice yourself, once you’ve hand-written enough Kubernetes manifests: most real applications need the same handful of resource types, configured slightly differently depending on context, deployed repeatedly over the life of a project. Helm just formalizes that pattern instead of leaving you to solve it yourself with copy-paste and careful attention. That’s really the same underlying theme running through this entire series — Kubernetes gives you precise, powerful primitives, and the tools built on top of it (Services routing by label, controllers enforcing desired state, and now Helm templating repeated structure) exist because doing everything manually, correctly, every single time, at scale, simply isn’t realistic for a human to sustain. Have you built your own Helm charts yet, or are you still mostly consuming existing ones from public repositories? What finally pushed you to make that jump? What Is Helm? The App Store for Kubernetes (Kubernetes Package Manager) was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Helm packages entire Kubernetes applications — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and more — into reusable, templated charts you can install with one command. Here’s what Helm actually does, how charts work, and when raw YAML is still the better choice.

That’s a completely reasonable way to learn what each piece actually does.
